title: Tax scheme
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE Hyderabad SITE Association of Trade and Industry has formally endorsed new measures introduced to ease regularisation of businesses, and urged local shopkeepers and traders to register with the FBR. It is not often that the private sector takes initiative in this regard. Registration will allow eligible retailers to avail themselves of FBR’s new Fixed Tax Asaan Scheme, introduced a few months ago to encourage unregistered businesses to enter the formal tax system. Under the scheme, eligible retailers with an annual turnover of up to Rs200m will pay a fixed tax of 1pc of gross turnover, subject to a minimum annual payment of Rs25,000. The scheme, introduced after the failure of the Tajir Dost Scheme, has been tailored to recommendations laid down after extensive consultations between the government and traders. It is, therefore, incumbent on the latter to use the opportunity to improve compliance.
Attempt after attempt to get retailers to register with the tax authorities has failed to deliver the desired results. Meanwhile, the taxman has placed a disproportionate burden on the documented economy, with the salaried sector alone contributing far more in income tax than the amount collected from retailers through relevant withholding taxes. According to provisional FBR tax figures for the last fiscal, income tax deducted from salaried individuals was Rs633bn, compared to about Rs70bn collected from retailers under two relevant withholding tax provisions. That imbalance has placed an unfair burden on those already within the documented economy, while allowing significant economic activity outside the tax net to remain undertaxed. This fiscal year, the government must enforce compliance consistently and fairly. The fiscal space it has available has been restricted for far too long because of lobbyists and pressure groups. It is commendable that trade leaders are now championing the Fixed Tax Scheme themselves, but if compliance remains low, the government must act. The new arrangement must not become another means of protecting one politically influential constituency from scrutiny while those already within the documented economy continue to shoulder a disproportionate share of the tax burden. The government has offered traders an easier route into the tax system; they must now reciprocate by registering and declaring their actual turnover, while the state must ensure that the rules are applied to everyone.
Published in Dawn, August 16th, 2026

title: The Middle East’s Nato?
author: none@none.com (Sikander Ahmed Shah)
content:
ON Aug 7, 2026, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye signed the historic Makkah Joint Defence Agreement (MJDA) to strengthen collective deterrence against external armed aggression. The agreement provides that an armed attack on one state would be regarded as an attack on all parties to the agreement. Historically, Pakistan has maintained long-standing defence ties with both countries. For example, Turkiye has supplied corvettes to Pakistan, while Pakistan has supplied training aircraft to Turkiye; Saudi Arabia, too, has purchased Turkish drones. Pakistan has also provided training and technical assistance to Saudi forces. Previously, Pakistan has entered into defence and military cooperation agreements with Saudi Arabia as well as other GCC countries.
MJDA is grounded in international law. Article 51 of the United Nations Charter recognises the inherent right to individual or collective self-defence when an armed attack occurs against a member state. Article 51, located in Chapter VII of the UN Charter, is the principal exception to the general prohibition on the threat or use of force in international relations established under Article 2(4) of the Charter, which protects the territorial integrity and political independence of states. Crucially, self-defence is triggered only by an “armed attack” establishing a high threshold for the lawful use of force.
In practice, states have used force in self-defence both after an armed attack and, more controversially, on a pre-emptive or anticipatory basis. Such force has been used unilaterally as well as collectively with allies. A prominent example of collective self-defence followed the Sept 11, 2001, attacks, when Nato invoked Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty for the first time. Article 5 provides that an armed attack against one or more Nato members is considered an attack against all, requiring each member to assist the state attacked, including through armed force where deemed necessary.
Controversial claims of collective self-defence have also arisen where a state has used force against another state purportedly in defence of a third state, in the absence of a mutual defence arrangement. One such case arose when the US used force against Nicaragua, claiming collective self-defence of El Salvador, alleging that Nicaragua was arming and assisting Salvadoran rebels fighting its government. The dispute ultimately came before the International Court of Justice in Military and Paramilitary Activities in and against Nicaragua.
The right to collective self-defence has, in practice, been invoked not only against other UN member states, but also against internal threats, or what has been interpreted as armed attacks attributed to terrorist groups and other non-state actors. Examples where states have requested foreign assistance as collective self-defence or, at a minimum, intervention by consent against internal threats, include the Syrian request for Russian assistance, and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government’s request from Saudi Arabia and its allies against the Houthis, the latter expressly invoking Article 51 of the UN Charter.
The Iraqi government also requested armed assistance against IS, providing the basis for states to invoke collective self-defence of Iraq against an international terrorist group. Iraq maintained that IS posed a serious threat to its people and territorial sovereignty. Moreover, the UN Security Council recognised IS as a threat to international peace and security.
The new trilateral security agreement raises questions about its costs for Pakistan.
Regarding global terrorism, the UN Security Council had earlier, somewhat controversially, recognised this position. Resolution 1368 (2001), adopted the day after 9/11, affirmed the inherent right of individual and collective self-defence in the context of those attacks. Resolution 1373 (2001) reaffirmed this right while strengthening global counterterrorism obligations. The US subsequently used force in Afghanistan under Article 51, while Nato separately invoked Article 5 of its collective defence pact.
Geopolitically, notwithstanding the potential benefits — including greater economic assistance from Saudi Arabia and other GCC states, and likely US support — the agreement raises questions about its costs for Pakistan and, more importantly, what Pakistan can realistically provide. Pakistan has consistently maintained that such arrangements would not extend its nuclear umbrella.
Practically, questions arise over how Pakistan could protect Turkish security interests, whether against Israel or internal threats from Kurdish separatist groups operating from Syria and Iraq. Regarding Saudi Arabia, reciprocal security guarantees may exist in theory, but their practical operation remains unclear. It is uncertain what meaningful military assistance Saudi Arabia could provide Pakistan in a conflict with India, with which it maintains close ties. More broadly, it is unclear what security benefits Pakistan would receive in return. The agreement could also draw Pakistan into a more direct confrontation with Israel, which has long maintained close defence ties with India and could further strengthen them in response.
The agreement also risks placing Pakistan at odds with Iran, with which it shares a long border and has at times cooperated against cross-border security threats. Involvement in a conflict with Iran over Middle Eastern security could further destabilise Pakistan’s western frontier while relations with Afghanistan and India remain tense and conflict-ridden. Pakistan has accused both states of facilitating terrorism and undermining its security. Moreover, Pakistan has the world’s second-largest Shia population after Iran. Any conflict with Iran could potentially strain internal cohesion and intensify sectarian tensions that Pakistan already struggles to contain.
Finally, if Pakistan is willing to enter mutual-defence pacts, why not prioritise one with China, which has major economic interests in Pakistan through CPEC and a strong stake in safeguarding this country’s external security? Such an arrangement could be mutually beneficial and deter further Indian adventurism, particularly given the effectiveness of the Pakistan-China defence cooperation and China-origin military systems during the four-day May 2025 Pakistan-India clash.
Historically, Western states have acquiesced in Pakistan’s possession and maintenance of nuclear weapons, largely in the context of its rivalry with India and stated self-defence needs. However, deeper integration into Middle Eastern and broader global security frameworks could generate greater Western pressure, including through international institutions, to constrain Pakistan’s nuclear weapons, missile technology and ballistic programmes. Such pressure could directly threaten Pakistan’s sovereignty and security. Lastly, the agreement could draw Pakistan’s armed forces into conflicts in which the country has historically maintained neutrality. Such commitments could stretch military resources, create fatigue, and increase vulnerability to Indian or Afghan opportunism and adventurism. 
The writer is a professor of law at Lums.
Published in Dawn, August 15th, 2026

title: Governance test
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
EVER since the interior minister called for smaller administrative units to improve governance, the question of new provinces has become the subject of much discussion. The proposal has revived a long-standing debate: does Pakistan need more provinces or greater devolution to the local level? A recent discussion in Islamabad on the topic brought together politicians, policymakers, technocrats and civil society representatives. While some participants supported the creation of new provinces, the broader sentiment appeared to favour, and rightly so, the decentralisation of political, administrative and financial power through effective local governments. The case for smaller provinces rests on the view that large administrative units have become unwieldy due to racing population numbers and the concentration of authority in a few urban centres. Proponents of this view argue that smaller provinces will bring governance closer to citizens and address the challenges. Yet even they recognise that any restructuring must reflect the will of the people and follow the constitutional process. This is vital to ensure that boundary changes do not become an exercise in political engineering, but emerge from genuine public demand.
However, Pakistan’s problem is less a shortage of provinces than excessive centralisation of every kind of power. Without empowered LGs and devolved resources, creating new provinces will not improve governance. The more immediate task should be to make LGs genuinely functional. After all, citizens turn most often to elected representatives over basic issues such as roads, streets, sewerage and other necessary municipal services. These are the challenges that should be addressed at the local level. Sadly, because of the political ambitions of the ruling elite, LGs in Pakistan have intentionally been denied adequate administrative and financial powers. The outcome is a distorted structure in which provincial governments perform functions that should be handled much closer to the citizens. This results in political patronage, administrative congestion and poor service delivery.
The debate therefore rightly widened the reform agenda. Judicial and electoral reforms, intra-party democracy, the rule of law and institutional behaviour cannot be separated from the question of good governance. As some participants noted, changing boundaries without reforming the underlying political and institutional culture will only lead to the same governance failures. New provinces may, where there is genuine public demand and a sound administrative and fiscal case, form part of a broader governance restructuring. But the first test is whether power is actually transferred to the citizens. We need governments that are closer to the people, more accountable and financially empowered. The aim should not be to redraw Pakistan’s map. It should be to redraw the relationship between the state and its citizens.
Published in Dawn, August 15th, 2026

title: National security odyssey
author: none@none.com (Ali Tauqeer Sheikh)
content:
WHEN Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi recently declared that national security requires deep reforms, and ISPR publicly endorsed the call, both were arguing for the same things: coherence, coordination, service delivery pushed closer to the doorstep, a state that functions as a state should. Nothing wrong with that ambition. The problem is what it left out, and how familiar that omission is.
Pakistan has set out for this destination before. Every serious reset since 1947 has restated some version of that list: Peace. Prosperity. Rule of law. A federation the provinces actually believe in. None of it was ever the wrong destination. What keeps happening is Odysseus’s wandering. His ship knows exactly where Ithaca lies and still takes the long way, blown off course by whichever storm is loudest that year. Each course correction adds distance instead of closing it. This is not a nation still discovering what it wants. It is a nation that has known the address for decades but keeps failing to arrive.
    
Climate change is the clearest evidence of that failure, the one threat that has already reshaped the economy and governance more than any militant group, hostile neighbour, or political crisis since 2010. Yet, it barely features in the national security conversation beyond a meek reference in the 2021 National Security Policy. Pakistan’s own climate finance planning puts annual investment need at roughly $56.6 billion, one and a half times what defence and debt servicing cost combined, nearly 20 times the federal development budget. Climate investment is deferred, year after year, for the next government or generation to absorb.
The reason is structural, not a matter of neglect. Hydrological volatility asks a different set of questions than the ones conventional threats ask. A flood breaches an embankment, and the people who decide whether that embankment holds are provincial irrigation engineers. An evacuation is run by a district administration working off exposure lists, not from provincial headquarters. Urban flooding is a municipal failure before it becomes a national one, a drainage line that was never cleared. The Constitution already assigns disaster management, water, agriculture and local infrastructure to the provinces. National security planning grew up answering more conventional and transboundary threats. A constitutional division of labour has put the actual climate mandate one or more levels below where the security doctrine is written.
Each course correction adds distance instead of closing it.
Naqvi’s critics have already converged on the obvious corrective, but have failed to offer a political economy analysis: why has local government never taken root? Pakistan has built it three times, Ayub’s Basic Democracies, Zia’s local bodies, Musharraf’s LGO 2000 — all three imposed by military leaders, all three the same design: an election without power, a base for the man at the top, no foundations underneath. Civilian governments never fixed this. The reign of top-down development has continued. Each time reform came up, provincial and federal legislators were lured by the discretionary schemes that let them decide what gets built and funded in their constituencies. A local politician’s power comes from controlling those schemes, and real local government would take that power away. This has replaced planning with ad hocism, turning much of the PSDP into an investment in random, uncoordinated allocations rather than resilience. Local government cannot consolidate, and climate vulnerability cannot be addressed, until this political economy architecture is dismantled.
    
As long as politicians control allocations to their own constituencies, neither local government nor climate resilience gets to compound the benefits. Only the losses do.
Pakistan’s fiscal policy has run the same choice for decades: squeezed development budget on terms set by lenders, or populist spending. Climate resilience loses either way, cut first under austerity because it produces no immediate political return, and starved again under populist spending because discretionary schemes absorb whatever fiscal space survives. Flood protection spending is patchy, addressed only after a flood has already caused the damage.
Elite capture runs well past the PSDP and local government. The automobile sector sits behind tariff walls, shielded from competition. Circular debt in the hydrocarbon energy sector is never resolved, only refinanced at a higher cost each time. Independent fossil-fuel power producers collect capacity charges regardless of what the country actually uses, a guaranteed return baked into the same contracts feeding the circular debt spiral. Undervalued official real estate rates let landowners dodge capital gains and wealth tax, channelling investment into speculative housing societies rather than production. And government borrowing crowds out private credit: banks holding government debt earn a safe return and have little appetite left to lend to the SMEs that would otherwise finance flood-resistant infrastructure or NAP and NDC implementation, the same SMEs that take the direct hit when a flood wipes out inventory or halts production. None of this is hidden: protected manufacturers, power producers, landowners, and captive banks are confident that the system built to check them answers, in practice, to them.
None of this invalidates the proposed reforms. But the reforms do not touch what has broken Pakistan’s economy and governance repeatedly, nor do they restore the local government capacity that decades of centralising incentive have deliberately eroded. Floods have destabilised the country more than insurgencies have. A weak district administration has cost more in a monsoon season than most internal security lapses cost in a year. A reform agenda that does not start there is not incomplete. It is aimed at the wrong problem, and it is one more course correction that adds distance instead of closing it.
The demand for structural national security reform is correct. The deepest reform available is recognising that Pakistan’s reform agenda does not begin with creating economically unviable administrative units, but with building hubs of performing local government first, units earned through capacity rather than drawn on a map. It will be a decades-long electoral process, building the capacity to manage administrative units before creating more of them. The state has seen its Ithaca before and sailed past it, more than once. Climate resilience and functioning local government both are fundamentally national security questions. This odyssey ends only when the doctrine comes home to the districts it has spent decades avoiding.
The writer is a climate expert.
Published in Dawn, August 13th, 2026

The deliberate failure of local governments to take root due to the political economy of discretionary funds controlled by federal and provincial legislators directly undermines climate resilience and effective service delivery.

title: Democracy and the market
author: none@none.com (Khurram Husain)
content:
EVERY decade in Pakistan’s history has seen a moment when a robust defence of democracy as the best form of government for a country like ours is needed. The never-ending struggle for supremacy between the democratic and non-democratic forces make it necessary. One of the key ways in which non-democratic forces advance their argument is to amplify all the bad things that happen under democratic rule, and all the flaws that democratically elected leaders bring to their position. They advance the idea that a more selfless leadership will be better for the country since it will put the national interest above its own. This is the central argument which numerous non-democratic forces have used to try and justify their intervention in politics and governance.
But there is a flaw in this premise. No leadership is selfless. Not in the political arena. Every contender for leadership emerges only by harnessing the powers inherent in society. Non-democrats, for example, have had the organised power of their respective institution behind them. And therefore, they have not been able to operate outside the limits set by their own affiliation with the institution that supplied them with the power to rule and to attack other institutions — which cannot, by any stretch of the imagination, be seen as selfless actions taken for the sake of the country.
    
In fact, to use the words of Hamilton in the Federalist Papers — the founding documents of the American system — democracy is predicated on the idea that human beings, or at least those who seek power and thereby become players in the political arena, are “ambitious, vindictive and rapacious”. The idea that people (or at least those who enter the arena of politics) are inherently selfish, self-serving, rapacious and ambitious was ingrained in the philosophical traditions from which democracy arose.
Hume wrote that, when devising a system of rule, “every man ought to be supposed a knave, and to have no other end, in all his actions, than private interest”. Montesquieu asserted that “[c]onstant experience shows us that every man invested with power is apt to abuse it … it is necessary from the very nature of things that power should be a check to power”. Kant took the argument even further, effectively saying that it should be possible to build a system of rule even for a nation of devils, because a rightly arranged constitution forces their selfish inclinations to check one another, producing an outcome identical to what good moral character would have produced.
Both democracy and the market are designed to harness the worst motivations of individuals — towards the pursuit of the common good of all.
The list goes on and on. Democracy is premised on the idea that rulers will bring bad motivations to their position, and it works on this premise to build a system where the separation of powers and the accountability and transparency that come with it will work to constrain these motivations, and channel them towards the collective good.
This is one foundational element that democracy has in common with the other big idea that emerged at around the same time: the market as the organising principle of economic life. The market also assumes that human motivations are greed and self-interest. When we meet greedy and self-interested people, most of us are usually not impressed. But taken collectively, the idea behind the market was to harness these energies towards the pursuit of the collective good. Both democracy and the market are designed to harness the worst motivations of individuals — towards the pursuit of the common good of all.
They aim to do this by pitting these bad motivations against each other and via a scheme of separation of powers where no single branch of government should exercise sway over the entire apparatus of state. Today, if there is any separation of powers left in the country, it is the federal versus the provincial governments. Little wonder that a demand materialises from silent places for undoing this as well.
When one points to the defects of individual democratic rulers, parties or governments, one should remember that non-democratic forms of government are not going to be without defects of their own. But they will be better at ensuring their defects are not amplified in the national conversation, so the common citizenry is left with the impression that only democratic rule has defects. The bigger problem is that non-democratic rulers, meaning those who come to the political arena via a route other than the ballot box, have no checks on their motivations, because they usually stand above the separation of powers and all mechanisms of accountability that any political system has. As such, their self-serving motivations get a free, unchecked rein; our own history bears witness that their periods of rule ended up doing lasting damage to Pakistan.
This is what must be kept in mind when working through the conversation these days around breaking up the provinces, or creating new ‘administrative units’. The first question to ask is ‘where is this demand coming from?’ Is it coming from below or above? There is a demand, for instance in south Punjab to create a new province and that demand has been acknowledged by all three major democratic parties in the country today. But where is the demand in the rest of the country?
The bottom line is this: if the demand to restructure the federation is not coming from below, then it should not be pursued. The federation is not a toy to be played with, and not someone’s snack to be cut up into bite-sized nuggets because a handful of people think that by doing so some kind of benefit will follow.
The writer is a business and economy journalist.

whyMatters: This article offers a unique philosophical defense of democracy, positing that it is designed to harness self-interest for the common good, unlike unchecked non-democratic systems. summary: Pakistan's history shows a continuous struggle between democratic and non-democratic forces, with the latter often amplifying democratic flaws while claiming selfless motives.
The premise of 'selfless leadership' advanced by non-democratic forces is flawed; all contenders for power, including non-democrats, operate from inherent self-interest.

Democracy, much like the market system, is fundamentally designed to harness selfish human motivations and channel them towards the collective good through mechanisms like separation of powers and accountability.
Non-democratic rulers, by operating above checks and balances, allow their unchecked self-serving motivations to inflict lasting damage, as evidenced by Pakistan's history.

title: New regional security order
author: none@none.com (Zahid Hussain)
content:
THE triangular defence pact signed last week by Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan is the most consequential geopolitical development reshaping the strategic landscape of the region and beyond. It has been concluded in the midst of a war that not only affects the region but also has far-reaching implications for the wider world. The three countries span the Middle East, South Asia and Europe.
Despite facing diverse security challenges, they are bound together by a common defence pact. While Saudi Arabia and Pakistan were already bound by a bilateral agreement signed last year, Turkiye’s entry has broadened the scope of the pact. The collective strength of these three countries has made the grouping a formidable force in the region.
    
Although the full text of the Makkah Joint De­­fence Agreement has not been made public, it do­­es declare that “any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an atta­­ck against them all”. It also states that the pact is not directed against any country but serv­­es as a deterrent against external aggression. It is, however, silent on the question of where the common threat lies.
This question becomes all the more pertinent as the triangular agreement has taken shape while America’s war on Iran drags on and Israel continues its expansionist war, threatening regional security. While Saudi Arabia has been directly affected by the war, Pakistan and Turkiye have remained on the fringes. The Makkah Agreement is being viewed as similar to Nato’s Article 5, but any military response would still require political decision-making. The immediate practical emphasis may be on intelligence-sharing and deterrence.
It is wrong to brand the newly formed defence bloc a Muslim alliance or, more narrowly, a Sunni one. It represents an emerging regional security architecture that reduces dependence on the US and pushes back against Israel’s expansionist agenda. Other Gulf countries — which have borne the brunt of Iran’s retaliation targeting US military bases on their soil — could also join the grouping.
The Makkah Agreement has fundamentally altered the strategic landscape of the region.
Questions have been raised about the reliability of the US as a defence guarantor for its Middle Eastern partners. Instead of ensuring security, the presence of US military bases has made these countries — many of which also have security pacts with Washington — more vulnerable. Lessening this dependence, however, does not mean severing ties with America.
    
All three countries maintain good relations with Washington, despite President Donald Tru­mp having destabilised the region through his unprovoked war on Iran and his continued support for Israel’s expansionist agenda. There has been a curious silence in Washington over the alliance.
Egypt was another country expected to join the grouping. The North African country has been part of a quad alongside these three allied nations, helping to find a negotiated resolution to the conflict. Cairo is believed to have reservations, however, about joining a regional security architecture that could affect its peace treaty with Israel. According to some analysts, Cairo appears to view the pact as much a political instrument as a military one. The group remains hopeful that Egypt will join the defence pact at some stage.
Further complicating matters is Iran’s mixed reaction to the agreement. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted a message calling on Muslim states to stand together, describing the moment as one in which they should rely only on themselves and embrace true brotherhood. The post left it unclear whether he was referring to the trilateral agreement.
Earlier, Araghchi is also reported to have said that Tehran was ready to partner with Persian Gulf states to build a new regional security architecture, arguing that recent events had demonstrated the need for regional countries to take responsibility for their own security. He said any security framework should include economic cooperation and stressed that military powers from outside the region should be excluded.
Meanwhile, Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of parliament’s national security committee, said that the “Saudis should understand that a paper agreement with Turkiye and Pakistan will not bring them security, just as decades of one-sided dependence on the Americans failed to do so”, thus reflecting the scepticism over the agreement among certain sections of the Iranian leadership. However, as reported, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman said that “the pact reflected a changing regional perception of US and argued that countries in the region could no longer rely on Washington”.
Predictably, the Makkah Agreement has provoked a strong reaction from Israel’s right-wing government, which views the development as a serious threat to its security. India has concerns over the triangular agreement, of which Pakistan is a key partner. According to some reports, the pact has accelerated the India-Israel security partnership.
On Aug 7, the day the trilateral agreement was signed, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Israeli counterpart Benjamin Netanyahu discussed the Special Strategic Partnership between their two countries in a telephone call. The two countries had formally elevated ties to a Special Strategic Partnership for Peace, Innovation & Prosperity during Modi’s state visit to Israel this year. That visit produced concrete defence and technology agreements. According to the Israeli media, both leaders recognised that they now face a shared strategic challenge: a bloc combining Saudi money, Turkish drones and a nuclear-armed Pakistan.
The Makkah Agreement has fundamentally altered the strategic landscape of the region. But there are also questions about how the partnership will actually work, given the varied security concerns of its members. While agreeing to a joint defence strategy, each country also brings its own conflicts and security problems.
That raises the question of whether the partners would be drawn into one another’s conflicts. While Pakistan’s principal security threat comes from India, Turkiye, a Nato member, has long-running territorial disputes with Greece in the Aegean Sea. There is also a view that, in practice, the pact is more about Saudi Arabia’s immediate security concerns stemming from regional non-state groups than Turkiye’s or Pakistan’s. These are issues that will require a more coherent collective response. For all the questions it raises, the Makkah Agreement marks a decisive shift in how the region’s major powers conceive their own security.
The writer is an author and journalist.

title: Fidel’s century
author: none@none.com (Mahir Ali)
content:
FIDEL Castro would have been amused by an unexpected encomium from the belly of the beast on the eve of his birth centenary, which will be commemorated tomorrow. Even the title of last month’s US State Department 100-page diatribe, Cuba: The Capital of 21st Century Communism, could be interpreted as a tribute. Like much else in a report intended to make the case for state capitulation or capture, this is an egregious exaggeration. The idea, obviously, is to illustrate how a small Caribbean island has posed an unacceptable threat to US ‘national security’ for nearly 70 years, and why that nuisance must be eliminated. Yet the supporting text is not mere fiction. Chunks of it could be read as an explanation for why Cuba proved so influential internationally in the decades after the 1959 revolution spearheaded by Castro.
A few examples from the report follow: “While Soviet communism was frequently driven by more practical great-power concerns … its Cuban successor was built around a near-singular obsession with the ‘liberation’ of the Global South from its Western colonial oppressors. In the minds of the Cubans, there was only one path to this goal: the destruction of the Yankee imperialist regime.” This ‘obsession’ deserves a red salute.
It acknowledges that “the Cubans were never just a Soviet proxy”, that “the Cuban Marxist project not only survived, but thrived” following the USSR’s demise and China’s turn towards capitalism, and that “Castro’s ideological project now enjoys something approaching ideological hegemony in leftist circles both within and beyond the West”. Apart from Washington’s hege-morons, no one associates the concept of hegemony, ideological or otherwise, with Cuba — except as an appropriate target in its internationalist endeavours over the decades.
A US report has inadvertently honoured Castro’s legacy.
Yet it’s hard to disagree with the report’s contention that “For the Western left — particularly in the United States — Cuba was the harbinger of a new kind of revolution. It was animated by a missionary zeal that Moscow had long since forgotten, and offered a novel theory of struggle and liberation”. As evidence, it cites the concept of ‘tercermundismo’, or ‘Third Worldism’, and highlights the 1966 Tricontinental Conference in Havana as “a foundational event in the inauguration of [this] global revolutionary project” that brought together anti-imperialist representatives from 82 nations across Asia, Africa and Latin America. (The Pakistani Committee of Afro-Asian People’s Solidarity is cited as one of the participants.)
“In Cuba’s telling,” the report claims, “the oppressed peoples of the world ... all shared one enemy … Yankee imperialism.” That’s not far from the truth. It notes that in urging “revolutionaries to open up a hundred fronts of war against the American empire”, Che Guevara in his message to the conference was urging on not just rebels in the Global South but also “American radicals in the belly of the beast”. It’s unlikely Che would have disputed that imputation. Neither he nor Fidel have challenged the claim that the Soviets “were speaking Third Worldism as a second language. The Cubans spoke it as their native tongue”. That could be explained by their direct experience of US imperialism in the six decades preceding Castro’s revolution.
The State Department report is aimed at maligning almost every progressive movement in the US — from the Black Panthers to Antifa — by linking it to Cuban influence. To the extent that is true, that would be a triumph for Havana. It also provides another cause for kudos by admitting that “a particular affinity for the cause of ‘Palestinian liberation’ was embedded in the founding anti-imperialist and an­­ti-Western cre­ed of the Cuban revolution”. That alone could be seen as an excellent re­­ason for supporting Cuba in its glo­bal endeavours as far away as southern Africa, where Havana’s contribution in Angola abbreviated the lifespan of Western-backed Pretorian apartheid, as Nelson Mandela acknowledged.
Cuba has often floundered on the domestic front, despite tremendous achievements in, inter alia, education and healthcare. During his first campaign, in 2016, Donald Trump declared, “I love the poorly educated.” Fidel Castro and his comrades detested the idea of any Cuban being poorly educated, and remedied the ignorance bred by their US-friendly predecessors. That partly explains Cuba’s resilience in the face of 65 years of economic and military aggression from the north. Its survival thus far amid the imperial denial of fuel, food and medicine has been nothing short of a miracle, but it’s not the first Cuba has accomplished.
Whatever Cuba’s fate, the memories of ‘fidelismo’ will linger, its ghost hovering over the latest spoils of US imperialism. And, sooner or later, history shall absolve him, as Castro predicted back in 1953.

An inadvertent US State Department report acknowledges Cuba's profound international influence, citing its role in foundational anti-imperialist events like the 1966 Tricontinental Conference and its affinity for causes like Palestinian liberation and anti-apartheid struggles in Southern Africa.

Cuba's domestic achievements in education and healthcare, coupled with its strong ideological resolve against 'Yankee imperialism,' partly explain its survival against decades of US-imposed economic blockades and sanctions.

title: More provinces or modernisation?
author: none@none.com (Syed Sardar Ali)
content:
FEDERAL Interior Minister Syed Mohsin Naqvi deserves praise for speaking in public what we all concede in private — that Pakistan is heading for a political and economic crisis unless we fundamentally change our course. Policymakers, legislatures, and career politicians see the crisis coming, but their private interests prevent them from broaching the subject.
It fell to a relatively newcomer to break the silence. The minister must be credited for casting the first stone. The minister highlighted two key failures. An ineffective state that cannot deliver basic services to its citizens and an anaemic economy that cannot generate sufficient tax revenues to finance the federal budget. The two problems have been festering for decades.
Successive democratic governments adopted the politically sensible strategy of ‘kicking the can down the road’. Now the problems have reached crisis proportions. In his warning shot, the minister beseeched the politicians to avert the impending catastrophe by jointly finding a solution.
The governance crisis is evident, most tragically, in the number of terrorist incidents. In 2026, Pakistan ranked first on the Global Terrorism Index, and was “the country most impacted by terrorism”. It is also one of the top 10 countries facing acute food shortages. According to the World Health Organisation, up to 55 per cent of Pakistan’s population lacks safely managed potable water. Because of malnutrition, nearly 40pc of children under five suffer from stunting. Nearly 36pc of school-age children are out of school.
The country ranks globally in the bottom 15-20pc of the World Justice Project Rule of Law Index, a consequence of deficiencies in security and pervasive corruption. The minister aptly described the country’s governance system as having “collapsed”.
The state’s lost capacity will not be regained by increasing the number of provinces.
Economically, Pakistan is at the bottom of the lower-middle-income band. Erratic growth since 2008 has pushed Pakistan below many of its South Asian neighbours in per capita GDP. Pakistan has run an annual budgetary shortfall for over 50 years.
The country runs an annual trade deficit of over $30 billion. Debt servicing consumes roughly 50pc of total tax revenues. With the current debt-to-GDP ratio hovering around 70pc, Pakistan is certain to miss the target of bringing the debt down to 50pc of GDP by financial year 2032-2033 as mandated by the Fiscal Responsibility and Debt Limitation Act. Pakistan has utilised 25 lending and financial support arrangements with the IMF, more than any other country in the world. Again, Naqvi is correct in describing Pakistan’s economic situation as unsustainable.
The weakest part of the minister’s speech, however, was not his identification of the problem but the solution. He asserted that we significantly increase the number of provinces. An increase in the number of administrative units, he implied, would bring public services to people’s doorsteps and result in the quick redressal of businessmen’s grievances. He, however, did not explain the causal link between the number of administrative units on the one hand and state effectiveness and robust economic performance on the other.
Afghanistan, approximately 25pc smaller than Pakistan in terms of area and 5.7 times smaller when measured by population, is divided into 34 provinces. Those who argue for more provinces cite Afghanistan as evidence. But Afghanistan is one of the poorest countries in the world with almost no modern state institutions. Canada, on the other hand, is 12 times bigger than Pakistan in landmass but has only 10 provinces. A member of the G7, Canada has a generous social welfare system. There does not appear to be any causal link between state effectiveness and economic progress and number of provinces.
The delivery of public services is one of the characteristics of a modern state. Other features include a monopoly on power, a standing professional army, the presence of a Weberian bureaucracy, ability to draw long-term plans, and the capacity to effectively enforce laws and policies.
In Pakistan, state effectiveness reached its peak in the first half of 1960s during the implementation of the Second Five-Year Plan. Democratic governments, beginning in the 1970s, destroyed state capacity through nepotism, corruption and patronage. Civil bureaucracy gradually lost its essence of impersonality, specialisation, merit, hierarchy of authority and a rational-legal basis. The state’s lost capacity will not be regained by increasing the number of provinces.
The majority of farmers in Pakistan remain engaged in subsistence agriculture. An agricultural economy cannot generate sufficient resources to sustain a modern state and a modern military. Western nations can fund social welfare programmes and keep large standing armies because of the surplus generated by their industrial economic base. The shift from an agricultural to industrial economy took centuries to complete in the West, starting with the Industrial Revolution. Only a handful of non-Western nations, mostly in East Asia, have been able to make this transition.
The emergence of a globally competitive industrial economy requires the presence of a host of enabling factors. The number of provinces is not one of them. Increasing the number of provinces, while keeping intact the current democratic framework, is unlikely to improve state effectiveness or boost economic output. It will not result in delegation of authority but in devolution of corruption, incompetence, and abuse of power. More provinces, however, may break the stranglehold of regressive political forces, tipping the balance of power in favour of the state. But the state must be administratively ready to reap the dividend at the centre. Pakistan suffers from lack of modernisation of its state, society, and politics. The country is poor because we have failed to transition from agricultural to industrial economy. These deep-seated structural problems cannot be solved by increasing the number of provinces. 
The writer has a background in public administration. He has worked with international financial institutions including the World Bank.
Published in Dawn, August 10th, 2026

title: Governance failures
author: none@none.com (Maleeha Lodhi)
content:
AN effort is underway to spark a debate on creating new administrative units in the country ostensibly on the grounds that the present system is not delivering. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, whose proximity to the establishment is well known, tried to make the case. Claiming the present governance system has “collapsed”, he called for more provinces and administrative units. He offered no explanation of what “collapse” meant and how new units would magically fix Pakistan’s problems. His proposal found backing from the military spokesman. He echoed the call, urged a system “reset” and endorsed the creation of new administrative units.
Such calls are, of course, not new. Every so often, this proposal surfaces, mostly from the establishment or other interested groups. But any sweeping change has never found traction among major political parties or the public at large. This time was no different. Naqvi faced criticism from across the political spectrum. Prominent ruling party leaders questioned his statement. The PPP’s Sindh chief minister, Murad Ali Shah, roundly rejected the creation of new provinces. Awami Tehreek leaders accused the interior minister of advocating Sindh’s division. Other parties argued that an “illegitimate” government had no authority to undertake such a move. The Lahore High Court Bar Association condemned Naqvi’s proposal as unconstitutional. Its office-bearers said those responsible for the destruction of the existing order were now proposing a “new system”.
    
The argument that Pakistan’s governance crisis is due to the number or size of its provinces simply doesn’t hold. One can make a case for administrative reorganisation on other grounds. For example, smaller units can bring government closer to the people. But that goal can be achieved by empowering local government. In any case, the Constitution lays out a clear process for making any changes to provinces. Naqvi’s proposal implied it can be done by executive fiat. Any change including altering the boundary of any province requires a resolution passed by a two-thirds majority in the relevant provincial assembly, followed by a constitutional amendment adopted by a two-thirds majority in both the National Assembly and Senate.
The timing of this debate is baffling. The debate is being initiated at a time when one province confronts an active insurgency, a second faces mounting militant violence, and Azad Kashmir is experiencing widespread protests and civil unrest.
There is a spurious connection between the provincial configuration and the governance crisis.
Those who draw a spurious link between Pakistan’s provincial structure and its governance failures lack historical perspective of why the country today is beset with so many serious, overlapping challenges. These challenges are the cumulative result of prolonged political instability, deferred economic reforms, visionless leadership, rule without law, and a consistent preference by successive governments for foreign engagements over unresolved, festering domestic problems. External overreach and internal underreach has been a consistent pattern. Governance is adversely affected by these factors. But it is elite capture that has been the most damaging.
    
Elite control of state power, of politics and much of the country’s resources has ensured elite interests consistently trump public interests. The power elite — a symbiotic nexus between political and military actors — has resisted meaningful reform and avoided tackling the economy’s structural problems — tax reforms, land reforms, reforms in governance. It has ‘rentier’ characteristics: using access to public office to leverage state resources for its own gain. Elite capture is principally why governance has broken down. This has left the country with interlocking crisis: state insolvency, insecurity, poverty, crumbling education and health systems, mounting energy shortages as well as environmental degradation. At the same time, the convergence between the country’s youth bulge, economic stagnation and the education deficit poses stark risks for the future.
A closer look at Pakistan’s governance failures shows political instability to be the core driver. The country has lurched between military interventions and civilian rule in a recurring cycle, punctuated by outbreaks of public protests demanding political change. This political discontinuity has prevented the emergence of a stable and predictable environment in which to address the country’s problems. It also entrenched a power asymmetry between elected and unelected institutions. In recent years, this produced a hybrid model of informal power-sharing between the civilian government and the military. That arrangement has now been supplanted by military dominance.
A major contributor to present challenges has been the persistent reliance by both civilian and military governments on dysfunctional and unsustainable economic policies. Rather than mobilise domestic resources, successive governments turned to borrowing and bailouts to cover widening budget and balance-of-payments deficits — the root of chronic financial crises. The country’s foreign alignments ensured steady access to economic aid and external funds. This ‘borrowed growth’ might have worked if the fiscal space had been used to fix structural problems. It wasn’t.
Instead, external financing, combined with high remittances, allowed ruling elites to paper over those problems and avoid reform. The failure to raise adequate domestic resources together with low levels of savings and investment led to increased borrowing and higher debt. This resulted in an economy that lurches from one IMF tranche to the next. Today Pakistan is stuck in a low-growth, low-investment, high-debt equilibrium trap that clouds its economic future. But the power elite refuses to change course.
Governance challenges have also been compounded by the repercussions of protracted foreign engagements, the dynamics of great power competition, and the fault lines of regional geopolitics. An implacably hostile India, unresolved Kashmir dispute, and an unstable Afghanistan pushed security to the top of the national agenda. But this involved a strategic trade-off. Defence spending and objectives were prioritised at the expense of economic development, social services and broader policy goals.
Elite interests, flawed policies, failure to reform, chronic instability and the headwinds from geopolitical storms are all drivers of Pakistan’s governance crisis. It is not the number of provinces or the administrative architecture that are the source of the crisis. Improvements in provincial efficiency and delivery are certainly needed. But to justify altering the Constitution’s provincial framework using disingenuous arguments does no service to the country.
The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.
Published in Dawn, August 10th, 2026

title: Wrong solution to the right problem
author: none@none.com (Ahmad Hassan)
content:
PAKISTAN’S governance crisis is fundamentally institutional rather than geographical.
While the creation of new provinces may address certain concerns relating to regional identity, representation, and administrative reach, it cannot by itself remedy systemic deficiencies in governance. Without meaningful institutional reform, decentralisation, and fiscal planning, new provinces risk reproducing existing problems at a greater administrative and financial cost.
Modern federal democracies increasingly function through a three-tier system of governance, in which constitutional authority is distributed among the federal government, provincial governments and elected local governments. The rationale is both democratic and practical; decisions should be taken at the lowest level capable of addressing them effectively.
National defence and foreign affairs belong to the federation, provincial policy belongs to the provinces while matters such as municipal services, sanitation, local infrastructure and community development are most effectively managed by local governments. This principle of democratic decentralisation ensures that government remains closer, more responsive and more accountable to the people.
Pakistan’s Constitution already embraces this model. Article 140A requires provinces to establish local governments and devolve political, administrative and financial responsibility to elected local representatives.
In other words, the Constitution already provides a mechanism for bringing government closer to the people. The challenge, therefore, is not the absence of a constitutional framework but the failure to implement it meaningfully.
    
Unfortunately, Pakistan’s experience has often been the opposite. Local governments have frequently been weakened, dissolved or deprived of meaningful financial autonomy, while development funds and administrative authority remain concentrated at the provincial level.
This is, in part, a consequence of the political incentive structure within provincial governance. Meaningful devolution inevitably reduces the concentration of power, resources and political visibility enjoyed by the provincial leadership, creating little incentive to transfer genuine authority to local institutions.
The consequence is a constitutional distortion. Members of the provincial assemblies, instead of focusing on legislation, policy formulation, executive oversight and public finance, increasingly involve themselves in roads, schools, local development schemes and other matters of municipal administration.
Legislators are elected to make laws and hold the executive accountable, not to perform functions that properly belong to elected local governments. When legislative institutions assume executive responsibilities, both governance and lawmaking suffer.
The question is whether good governance will be achieved by creating more provinces or by strengthening the institutions that already exist.
Before creating additional provinces, Pakistan must therefore ask why the existing constitutional model of local government has not been fully implemented. If governance is the primary objective, strengthening local governments may prove to be a more effective and less costly reform than creating entirely new provincial structures.
Another aspect that merits consideration is the financial implications of creating new provinces. A province is not merely a new chief minister and provincial assembly. It requires a complete governmental framework, including a high court, provincial secretariat, public service institutions, tax authorities, police administration, regulatory bodies, specialised departments and thousands of public servants. These institutions create permanent financial obligations in terms of salaries, pensions, infrastructure and operational costs.
    
The question is not whether Pakistan can create new provinces. It can. The question is whether the anticipated governance benefits justify the substantial administrative and financial costs.
Another important consideration is economic sustainability. Many proposed provinces, particularly less industrialised regions, possess significant agricultural potential but limited industrial and service-sector capacity. Without a diversified economic base, newly created provinces may remain heavily dependent on federal transfers for their survival. Therefore, any restructuring of provincial boundaries must be preceded by serious fiscal analysis.
This is not an argument against creating new provinces. It is an argument that constitutional restructuring must be accompanied by institutional and financial planning.
The identity dimension of this debate must also not be forgotten. For many communities, demands for new provinces are not only about administration but also about recognition, representation and political inclusion. Historical regions such as Bahawalpur and Hazara have long sought acknowledgment of their distinct identities. Such aspirations cannot simply be dismissed.
However, political representation must translate into actual improvement in the lives of citizens. Creating new provinces may provide opportunities for regional leadership and address feelings of exclusion, but changing boundaries alone cannot resolve deeper issues of governance, economic opportunity, institutional capacity and public service delivery.
Pakistan’s governance challenges require a comprehensive approach. Strong local governments, professional civil services, transparent administration, fiscal responsibility and constitutional continuity are the foundations of effective governance.
    
If, after meaningful reforms and careful fiscal assessment, parliament concludes that additional provinces are necessary, such decisions should be taken on constitutional and administrative grounds rather than political expediency.
Pakistan undoubtedly needs better governance. The question is whether that objective will be achieved by creating more provinces or by strengthening the institutions that already exist.
The problems undermining governance are not merely products of geography. Before redrawing the map, we should first reform the machinery that governs it.
The writer is a practising lawyer based in Lahore.

title: The supreme sacrifice
author: none@none.com (Afzal Ali ShigriTariq ParvezTariq Khosa)
content:
THE police are a vital pillar of our social fabric, serving not only as guardians of the law but also as protectors of the community, said President Asif Ali Zardari on Police Martyrs Day on Aug 4. “Their exemplary courage, firm dedication and ultimate sacrifice in the service of the nation will always inspire pride and command the deepest respect of every citizen of Pakistan,” he added. The prime minister, too, honoured the bravery of police officers who had laid down their lives in the line of duty, noting that the force displays “exceptional professionalism and unflinching resolve” in the nation’s fight against terrorism, violent extremism and crime.
The Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies reported that the first seven months of 2026 witnessed 2,786 deaths linked to terrorist violence and counterterrorism operations — 434 security forces’ personnel lost their lives, including 152 police officials in KP and 89 in Balochistan. So far, July has been the deadliest month of 2026, with 112 security officials offering the supreme sacrifice in the line of duty, compared to 38 fatalities a month earlier in June. This is an unprecedented 195 per cent increase in the deaths of law enforcers. 
At least eight suicide attacks were recorded last month, the highest number in a single month during the past decade. The recent deadly attack near a police station in Swat caused 17 fatalities. As this paper rightly asserted after the Swat bombing, it “is far too high a toll, and the state needs to urgently refine its CT strategy to prevent further loss of precious lives”.
Following Police Martyrs Day, one of us convened a forum of serving and retired police officers to discuss the current vulnerabilities and challenges faced by police in general, and those in KP and Balochistan in particular. The trajectory and tenor of violence in these provinces have distinct traits. KP has been on the receiving end since 9/11, paying a huge price in the so-called war against terror. Since Kabul’s takeover by the Taliban in August 2021, violence and bloodshed have assumed greater intensity. Acts of terror have risen exponentially, with fatalities among security forces and civilians progressively rising each year. The last two years have been the worst so far, with police losing 314 personnel.
The last two years have been the worst so far, with police losing 314 personnel.
Balochistan is facing its fifth (and longest) phase (20 years) of insurgency by separatists. Nawab Akbar Bugti’s killing in a cave near Kohlu in August 2006 was an unfortunate incident that led to a sharp escalation in Baloch militancy. The terrorist nexus of the BLA, BRA and BLF has added lethality to insurgent attacks. BLA’s Majeed Brigade is well-equipped and emulates TTP’s violent tactics. It has superior weaponry, indicating the role of hostile foreign agencies in fomenting unrest in the province. The police’s challenge has increased manifold now that the entire province has been converted into police jurisdiction. The gap in human resources, infrastructure and training for the job is pronounced. A recent significant development is the incursion of the TTP in the Pakhtun areas as witnessed in the tragic July 6 attack on the Mangi Dam pumping station police post by the terrorist group, leading to the kidnapping and killing of 27 policemen. Our deliberations have led to identification of certain vulnerabilities and constraints that beset the police operating in the terror and insurgency-prone areas of KP and Balochistan where violence is driven by a combination of enhanced militant capability, difficult terrain, cross-border dynamics and institutional challenges. The following issues are pertinent.
Intelligence coordination and information sharing: Coordination between police, intel agencies and other law-enforcement institutions is not always seamless; delays in sharing actionable intelligence reduce the ability to prevent attacks or intercept terrorists before they strike.
Inadequate protection of police personnel and infrastructure: Police stations, check posts and patrols are often targeted because they have limited physical protection, surveillance or early-warning capabilities; some units in dangerous zones lack sufficient protective equipment, secure transport and modern communication systems, increasing their vulnerability.
Limited capacity and community-based policing: In remote and conflict-affected areas, a trust deficit exists between communities and police. Without strong local engagement, authorities receive fewer timely reports about suspicious activities, allowing terrorist networks to operate with greater freedom.
The merger of Fata into KP and the conversion of ‘B’ areas into ‘A’ areas in Balochistan was undertaken without adequate planning, capacity building or the provision of necessary financial and operational resources. The denial of these essential resources has exposed both police and the civil armed forces to avoidable risks, contributing to a significant increase in casualties among personnel. Expressions of support and appreciation for their sacrifices must therefore be matched by meaningful investment in manpower, training, equipment, intelligence, mobility and welfare to enable police to perform their duties effectively and safely.
As former police chiefs we acknowledge that the challenges faced by current police commanders are far more daunting and require a strategic and operational rethink to restore order and promote peace in the restive borderlands in Pakistan’s north and south. Serving and retired police officers agree that the revised CT NAP must be implemented through professional tactics and strategic oversight. Here are a few recommendations at the operational level.
Strengthen intelligence-led policing: Establish integrated intelligence coordination mechanisms that facilitate timely information-sharing among police, intelligence services and local administration; expand analytical capabilities and use technology to identify emerging threats, while ensuring operations remain consistent with the law and human rights standards.
Modernise police protection and training: Upgrade security at vulnerable police facilities through better surveillance, convoy drills, ambush response, communications and sound infrastructure; provide regular training in CT tactics, drone threat response, incident command and officer safety, along with appropriate protective equipment.
Expand community policing and public partnerships: Build stronger relationships with local communities, tribal elders, religious leaders and CSOs to improve trust and encourage lawful reporting of suspicious activities; develop accessible mechanisms for citizens to share information confidentially; promote public awareness programmes that strengthen resilience.
The trend of rising terrorist attacks against, and thus higher casualties among, the police must be immediately stopped before it derails the entire CT effort in KP and Balochistan. This requires a balanced approach that combines effective policing, better intelligence coordination, professional training and meaningful community engagement. Strengthening these areas can enhance the safety of police personnel while also increasing public confidence and contributing to a more secure environment for local communities. Finally, for the policymakers and political leadership, our message is simple: invest in police and trust them to deliver. 
The writers are former inspectors-general of police.

title: Before AI hits the grid
author: none@none.com (Mahwish Khan)
content:
PAKISTAN’S announcement that it would allocate 2,000 megawatts of electricity for Bitcoin mining and AI data centres has triggered a predictable debate: can the country afford to supply that much power? It is an important question, but not the most useful one. Bitcoin mining, AI training and real-time digital services do not exactly place identical demands on the electricity system.
Pakistan’s electricity challenge is about more than the amount of generation capacity available. It is about when and where electricity is needed, whether the network can deliver it reliably, and how that demand is managed during periods of stress. During the hottest months, cooling demand pushes the grid towards its limits. At other times, generation capacity remains underused. But nationally available capacity does not automatically translate into reliable electricity at the location and hour a data centre requires it. Transmission constraints, substation capacity and power quality matter just as much as the headline allocation.
The better question is this: how should this new demand be designed and integrated into the electricity system from the outset?
Data centres are not ordinary consumers. Their location, cooling systems, computing equipment and grid connections are decided before construction begins. That gives Pakistan a rare opportunity to shape a major new category of demand before it becomes embedded in the system. But doing so requires recognising that not all computing demand is the same. Some services are highly sensitive to delay. User-facing AI applications, financial platforms and communications systems may require continuous availability. Their loads cannot simply be switched off whenever the grid comes under pressure. Other workloads may offer more flexibility. Certain forms of data processing and model training can be scheduled within broader time windows, distributed across locations or paused at planned checkpoints, depending on how the systems are designed.
Pakistan’s electricity challenge is about more than the amount of generation capacity available.
Where genuine flexibility exists, it can be reflected in tariffs and connection agreements. Eligible workloads could be scheduled outside critical peak hours. Operators could provide more accurate demand forecasts, limit abrupt changes in consumption, or use storage to reduce pressure on the network during short periods of stress. This is not a hypothetical mechanism. The UN referred to Ireland as a “cautionary tale” when the country faced a severe energy crisis because data centres consume roughly 23 per cent of the nation’s total electricity — nearly rivalling the power used by all residential homes combined. Ireland’s grid operator now assesses new data centre connections in constrained areas partly on whether the applicant can prove its demand is flexible, and writes that commitment directly into the connection agreement rather than leaving it voluntary. Pakistan can build the same discipline in from the start, instead of retrofitting it once the grid is already under strain, the way Ireland had to.
Pakistan does not need to begin from scratch. The country already has a cloud-governance and accreditation framework. The Cloud Office is mandated to set standards and compliance requirements for cloud service providers, while the existing accreditation criteria cover security, service availability, resilient power infrastructure and recognised data centre certification.
What the framework does not yet fully address is how efficiently these facilities use electricity and water, or how they interact with the wider power system.
The Ministry of IT & Telecom’s own concept note identifies this gap. It notes that the current framework does not explicitly prescribe standards for energy management, environmental performance, power usage effectiveness, water usage effectiveness or renewable energy integration. It proposes a national sustainability framework for data centres to fill that gap. That is the right direction. But the framework should go one step further by connecting digital-infrastructure planning with power sector planning.
Large facilities should provide credible forecasts of their electricity and water demand. Projects should be assessed against local network capacity, not simply national generation figures. Energy and water performance should be measured consistently. And tariffs should reward verified efficiency and flexibility rather than merely offering cheap electricity to large consumers.
This is not anti-investment. Serious data centre investors already consider reliable power, cooling, environmental compliance and long-term energy security when choosing markets. Good standards are not a barrier to investment, but rather, a part of a credible investment proposition. The first generation of AI infrastructure will shape the one that follows. Early decisions on location, efficiency and grid connection will become precedents that are harder to change once major investments have been made.
Pakistan does not need to wait for its grid to buckle before it asks this question, the way Ireland did. It has the chance to design demand before it hits the grid, not renegotiate it after the fact. 
The writer is director, Awareness and Outreach, National Energy Efficiency & Conservation Authority.
Published in Dawn, August 8th, 2026

title: Danger ahead
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PAKISTAN has already paid a heavy human price this monsoon, even as another dangerous spell approaches. NDMA figures covering June 26 to Aug 7 record 151 deaths — 73 of them children — and 448 injuries, besides damage to more than 1,200 houses and dozens of bridges and kilometres of roads. Chitral shows how quickly such destruction multiplies into other emergencies. Glofs, cloudbursts and flash floods have washed away bridges and severed roads, leaving communities unable to reach healthcare. Attendance at Lower Chitral’s district headquarters hospital has fallen by around 55pc, while patients from some isolated villages have stopped arriving altogether. Doctors are already reporting gastroenteritis and dysentery and fear outbreaks of typhoid and malaria. Pregnant women unable to reach hospitals face particular danger, while post-traumatic stress is emerging among disaster-hit communities. The situation shows us how extreme weather kills not only through torrents and collapsing homes, but also by cutting people off from medicines, clean water and timely treatment.
NDMA, Rescue 1122, district administrations and the National Highway Authority have been involved in evacuations, relief distribution and restoration work. But each disaster exposes the distance between issuing warnings and protecting people. Chitral residents have complained of slow road clearance, delaying access to villages where medical needs are mounting. Warning equipment in parts of KP has previously been damaged or stolen, pointing to weaknesses in maintenance and local ownership. District authorities must know which settlements require evacuation, where residents will be taken, how alerts will get to people without mobile connectivity and how food, medicines and medical teams will reach communities. Such plans must be prepared before an emergency, not improvised after valleys are cut off. Medical camps, safe-water points and emergency stocks should be positioned in vulnerable valleys.
There is particular urgency now. PMD’s Aug 7 outlook warns of moderate to heavy rainfall over the upper catchments of all major rivers from Aug 10 to 13, including KP, GB, Azad Kashmir, Islamabad and upper Punjab, with river and tributary flows expected to rise. Authorities should use this window to pre-position heavy machinery, boats, temporary bridges, fuel, food, drinking water, medicines and mobile clinics. Pregnant women, elderly people and patients requiring regular treatment should be identified for early evacuation, while alternative communication systems must be ready where conventional networks may fail. Shelters should be accessible and evacuation routes communicated before conditions deteriorate. Pakistan cannot control the monsoon or the instability of its glaciers. But it can control how seriously it acts on warnings. With the warning already given, the task now is to ensure that the next spell does not deepen an already heavy human toll.
Published in Dawn, August 8th, 2026

title: Israeli impunity
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
ANY hope that Hamas’s decision to disarm would lead to a breakthrough has been dashed for one simple reason: Israeli impunity. Tel Aviv has reacted to the Palestinian group’s announcement by saying it would not withdraw from Gaza until there was ‘genuine’ disarmament. What this actually means is that Israel has no intention of ending the occupation. Frustration at the Zionist state’s intransigence has been expressed by eight Muslim states, including Pakistan, that recently issued a statement condemning Tel Aviv’s violence in Gaza. Israeli attacks on health facilities and civilian targets were particularly highlighted in the statement, whose signatories include Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Turkiye. According to Unicef, Israel has killed 300 children over the last 300 days. Such a ‘ceasefire’, the UN agency said, “is failing children”. Meanwhile, the situation in the occupied West Bank is not any better, with violent settler attacks continuing. The settler community in Israel is known for its extremism and use of violence against Arab civilians. They aim to uproot the Palestinians from their ancestral lands and cement the occupation. While the Israeli state claims to investigate such attacks, this means little when rabid supporters of the settler movement sit in the cabinet. The statement by Muslim states also highlighted the situation in the West Bank.
The Muslim states have urged the UN Security Council to compel Israel to fulfil its obligations. This is wishful thinking, because if the UN and the international community had played their role, there would have been no campaign of extermination in Gaza, and the tens of thousands of Palestinians murdered by Israel since 2023 would have been alive today. If the Muslim world wants to end the carnage in Gaza and the West Bank, it must take practical steps against Israel, such as a diplomatic and trade boycott. Resolutions and condemnations will not save the Palestinians from Israeli terror. Moreover, President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace must be asked what it aims to do to make Israel honour the Gaza peace deal. It is clear that Tel Aviv does not intend to stop its murderous campaign in the Strip. The Palestinians have been making concessions for peace. It is now time Israel’s Western benefactors asked it to put its money where its mouth is.
