title: Threats all around
author: none@none.com (Dr Niaz Murtaza)
content:
WE are among the few states that have to contend with threats on all fronts: India to the east, TTP in the north, Afghanistan to the west and BLA in the south. Everyone agrees on the basic aim: defuse the threats to transform from a security state to a welfare state. The divide persists on strategy: between a military one that wins battles and a holistic one that fixes root causes and respects rights and laws that can lead to sustainable peace.
A holistic approach is most vital in Balochistan, now in the third decade of its fifth and longest insurgency. Focusing only on the kinetic aspect to quell terrorism misses a key point. Force alone doesn’t end threats. Violence recurs over the decades and lasts longer each time when neglect and abuse keep inciting anger and new recruits. Balochistan’s economic neglect is stark: it is our poorest region despite its small numbers, natural wealth and proximity to the rich Gulf states. It’s rich below the ground but poor above it. The political neglect goes back to the British era. Unlike in the case of other provinces joining Pakistan, Balochistan had no assembly vote/referendum on its status in 1947; its future was determined through elite consensus. This was despite its mix of unique traits — historical autonomy, distinct ethnicity and vast area — that led to initial talks on provincial status much before 1947, unlike for the princely states merged with the other provinces.
A public vote creates a strong bond that chiefs or militants can’t deny later. Balochistan lacked provincial status until 1970. Bahawalpur and Khairpur got elected assemblies in the 1950s. Oddly, learning no lesson from the 1971 debacle that the denial of democracy led to, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto removed Balochistan’s first elected set-up just 14 months after that tragic split. Military action followed. Such acts occurred later too. So, even in a state marked by autocracy, Balochistan stands out. Disappearances feed anger as do the jailing of key peaceful activists. Balochistan urgently needs a fairly elected and empowered set-up to tackle its issues. This may thin terrorist ranks. Limited force may then easily defeat radical elements unmoved by political change.
We must go beyond narrow policies.
The threats from Afghanistan and TTP are linked. TTP violence reflects extremism. However, many root causes feed it indirectly: legacies of Afghan wars, a militarised state’s past jihadist support and prolonged exclusion of tribal areas. The TTP has caused more deaths than BLA; its extremism precludes talks too. Yet, we must fix the root causes and respect rights and laws. This means precise intelligence-backed use of force in close liaison with locals, economic uplift and strong border checks without total trade and travel bans. It could mean rethinking cross-border attacks that may not stop incursions but may raise complex issues under UN laws and risk civilian deaths. We must also see the Afghan people as our main allies against the Afghan Taliban as they harm both of us greatly; rethink Afghan expulsions and treat those leaving voluntarily well. This may cut the number of Afghans the TTP now recruits. Afghan Taliban rigidity can be tackled by organising targeted sanctions along with regional and global powers.
Root causes are hard to fix soon given their complex nature in the conflict with India. But even managing symptoms will reduce the risk of nuclear war. Our wars no longer focus on land disputes but start after a terrorist attack next door, as in the Pahalgam atta­­ck in India-occupied Kashmir last year. Given the risks of a war using non-conv­entional means and the high bar under UN law for justifying cross-border attacks, both countries must pursue diplomacy.
Their interests and those of the wider world will be best served if they agree to a neutral UN mechanism that can review their existing evidence against each other, monitor future trends and facilitate urgent communication after an incident. This may help curb terrorism and water wars. Both Pakistan and India must also address the root causes of terrorism. Such trust-building steps may create an enabling environment for resolving more basic issues later bilaterally.
These threats are only a few flames in a bigger socioeconomic inferno we face. We must go beyond narrow policies that have fuelled the cauldron for long and employ the full spectrum of creative solutions that have helped many states douse similar conflagrations on a more durable basis.
The writer holds a PhD in political economy from the University of California, Berkeley, and has 25 years of grassroots to senior-level experience across 50 countries.

title: Politics is upon us
author: none@none.com (Arifa Noor)
content:
IT wasn’t an ordinary day by any stretch of the imagination, even though it began rather ordinarily. There was little news to interest anyone (and Kashmir was a no-no for television channels).
Initially, there came fleeting news about a press conference by the head of ISPR but it wasn’t meant to be. Those who had not been invited to the event thought the news was incorrect but later it transpired that the conference had been delayed to the next day, Friday.
And then came the bombshell — in Islamabad at an event hosting businessmen for a conference on the economy, business and all things complicated. Here, instead of the speeches by the men managing Pakistan’s finances (if there were any), it was Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi’s speech that got all the attention.
It’s still not clear why he spoke there but as the conference took place at a hall located close to his office, perhaps he offered to swing by and say a few words.
    
His speech didn’t just create headlines; it created an entire news cycle. In simple words, he confirmed in a way what the government’s worst critics have been saying — that people are in pain and the government hasn’t been able to provide them with any relief. He put it even more bluntly. He spoke of the ‘system’ (the entire country — not just the one in Sindh) having collapsed. Not collapsing but collapsed.
He said it wasn’t possible to deliver regardless of how hard the prime minister worked and how many long hours he put in. He referenced recent events in India, saying that if the ‘cockroaches’ (youth) got together, they would overthrow it all.
But more intriguingly, he also made it clear that giving people a few thousand rupees or a laptop wasn’t enough. This was clearly a reference to the various schemes launched by the PML-N as well as the Benazir Income Support Programme, which is seen as the PPP’s baby.
He proposed a solution by arguing the country needed more provinces or administrative units so that governance could be delivered at the doorstep. The next day, the DG ISPR reinforced this proposal.
The interior minister’s indictment of the present government will not be forgotten easily.
While his solution or proposal took no one by surprise, his criticism of the set-up did. After all, most of us are aware that there is much discussion behind closed doors on the need to revisit the NFC as well as the notion of devolution (which would assist the people as well as weaken the dynasty-controlled fiefdoms at the provincial level).
    
However, Naqvi’s indictment of the present government will not be forgotten easily — for now, all those who had been waxing lyrical about the work done by Maryam Nawaz in Punjab or by Shehbaz Sharif at the centre will find it hard to argue that the party has delivered and won over the people.
Interestingly, his remarks, which were a damning indictment of the current set-up, were initially met with silence. It took nearly a day before the reaction came from the PPP and PML-N whose public representatives are usually quick to hold media talks every day on any hint of criticism. But to contradict the interior minister, and one who is said to be very close to the highest in the establishment, is surely above the pay grade of those put in charge of information ministries.
Still, the senior tiers were called to report for duty. In Sindh, the chief minister himself pooh-poohed the suggestion, while from the PML-N Rana Sanaullah was the first to fire back. Since then, others too have joined the fray, but most of the criticism focuses on Naqvi and not those who back him.
There was also news of a family gathering at Jati Umrah in Lahore. Not much emerged from it other than some vloggers thundering about Nawaz Sharif having been woken up from his slumber — news that somehow didn’t get traction unlike Naqvi’s speech. Perhaps it is because the news is limited to a few who are relying on sources or because no one really believes the family is in a position to push back. The silence from the PPP heads is equally noticeable.
In the meantime, the lower tiers might continue to thunder, though it is hard to believe Mohsin Naqvi will now respond to these allegations. But what now seems inevitable is another amendment to the Constitution, even if there is little clarity on what it will bring. New provinces and other wholesale changes (for it would mean reconfiguring the Senate)? Or simply a strong local government system with some federal areas? Or will it begin with easing the provisions for creating new provinces? Or a change in the NFC? Nothing is clear but the path ahead seems to lead to parliament. That Ahsan Bhoon was also present at the event where Naqvi spoke also indicates this.
But while the powers that be have perhaps made their intentions clear, the silence from the parties means they are still to put together a strategy. Will they simply try to win over some concessions as they did during the previous two amendments? Will they drive a hard bargain? Or is the time and space for compromises over? The details are as above my pay grade as they are beyond the ability and position of Azma Bokhari or Atta Tarrar to respond to Naqvi. So as the hackneyed phrase goes, let’s wait and watch.
However, it might just be safe to say that the amendment will not sail through without hiccups. It would mean a weakening of both the parties vis-à-vis the provincial governments, politically as well as in terms of patronage. For instance, the PPP will lose its political raison d’être; for Maryam Nawaz, the position of chief minister might lose its lustre, increasing the competition for the position in Islamabad. The initial instinct therefore will be to bargain and get something in return, if they decide not to push back.
In other words, the hybrid system is now set for a new tug of war, which may leave some, if not all, of the stakeholders a little worse for wear.
The writer is a journalist.

title: Over-interpreting the youth
author: none@none.com (Jawed Naqvi)
content:
COCKROACH Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke revealed a crucial fact about himself to Newslaundry’s Manisha Pande. He said he had seen Shahrukh Khan’s 2002 movie Swades (‘My country’) many times over since he was a child and he finds it inspirational. So, I too switched on YouTube and saw it to the extent one could.
The story is about an Indian engineer at Nasa who misses home and goes on a visit to meet the lady who raised him upon his parents’ death in a car accident. The journey takes him to a village facing chronic power outages and where he also meets Kaveri Amma’s pretty ward Gita who is struggling to run a village school. So, the hero, while living out of a caravan trailer, builds a water reservoir from a tiny stream seeping from a rocky slope to ply a turbine he has assembled. The villagers get their steady power, leaving the hero to canvass support for the underprivileged children to join the struggling school. They do so by defying entrenched caste- and poverty-related odds.
The turbine event comes across as a band-aid for a country that has handed early dreams of affordable and universal healthcare to private buccaneers.
The state-run National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET) where corruption is rampant — which triggered Dipke’s Cockroach campaign — produces 137,000 doctors against 20 million applicants. Many who succeed go abroad to follow their dreams.
    
The phenomenon was seen as brain drain during the early years of India’s independence and there’s a news clip of Nehru on a US visit urging Indian professionals there to return home.
Dipke may have picked up the cue, but many others have returned to India over the years to work for the country’s progress.
The US-born human rights lawyer Sudha Bharadwaj was jailed for working among Chhattisgarh’s tribespeople to empower them with legal advice and moral support. Bharadwaj, currently out on stiff bail conditions, exchanged her American passport for Indian citizenship. She was arrested along with several young activists in 2020 for the crime of organising the Dalits and tribespeople to challenge the injustices they endured with the state’s connivance.
Rev Stan Swamy was an Indian Jesuit priest and tribal rights activist, the oldest person to be accused of terrorism in India. He died in a Mumbai prison at 83, a year after his arrest.
Dipke’s movement faces inevitable challenges ahead. Ground-breaking political changes are seldom if ever a clean shot.
Dipke may have seen Richard Attenborough’s award-winning movie Gandhi. Did he notice that B.R. Ambedkar or Bhagat Singh didn’t even get a walk-on part in the movie? That Ambedkar and Bhagat Singh featured in the Cockroach protests was reassuring. They had a well-grounded prognosis about what ailed Indian society.
Ambedkar, together with Periyar and M.G. Ranade had forcefully argued that social transformation must precede or accompany political freedom, famously maintaining that political independence without social equality was incomplete or a ‘lie’. Umar Khalid, Sharjeel Imam and Surendra Gadling are among the current crop of youth jailed for holding the torch passed on by an amazing generation of leaders.
Dipke’s movement faces inevitable challenges ahead. Ground-breaking political changes are seldom if ever a clean shot. It’s almost inevitable that there’s a Trotsky lurking to challenge Stalin in a leftist upheaval, or an Ernst Rohm paying dearly for over-interpreting his Fuhrer’s bloodlust. Likewise, leading the French Revolution, Robespierre sought to cleanse the leadership of opportunists. They ganged up to guillotine him instead.
Closer to home, Z.A. Bhutto was barely finished with Ayub Khan’s military rule when he waded into a far more momentous challenge from an estranged kindred spirit, a democrat this time in faraway Dhaka.
Indira Gandhi sought a clean break from corporate-feudal satraps within the Congress and garnered the left’s support against avaricious private bankers and assorted British-era princes. Then she was nudged by communal bigots still lurking in her party into a needless feud with the minority Sikhs, a grievous error that would eventually lay her low.
    
Rajiv Gandhi sought to lead India into a perfectly viable technology-savvy 21st century. He ended up balancing the party’s advice that thrust him between Hindu and Muslim communalists, one seeking to turn mythology into history, the other bent on stealing small change from a female divorcee.
Two earth-shaking upheavals in the 20th century nicely frame the context and reality of the youth-led Cockroach movement. The movement has already forced Narendra Modi’s education minister’s humiliating exit, rattling the bones of the faux muscular religio-fascist rulers. But what lies in store ahead for the lot when the exigencies of politics serve up crucial state polls next year in Uttar Pradesh and Punjab? Politicians would want to harness their energy to purposes that can neither be ignored nor trifled with.
The two important examples to better understand the Cockroach phenomenon perhaps rest in movements that led to India’s 1947 independence from Britain and Iran’s 1979 freedom from American control of the country.
The landmark events occurred barely 32 years apart. The Indian movement was set into motion in 1885 by professional ornithologist A.O. Hume. The Indian National Congress remained an elitist body until Gandhi turned it into a mass movement in 1920. It brought together a cornucopia of contradictions. Bhagat Singh and Lal Lajpat Rai were opposed to Gandhi’s nonviolence. While one was a votary of scientific socialism, the other was a staunch Hindu revivalist.
The Iranian Revolution was similarly led by competing groups of diverse ideological origins. The spine belonged to the experienced pro-Soviet Tudeh Party. The street craft was shored up by the Maoist Mujahideen-i-Khalq, but the masses were directed by highly politically savvy and well-read clergy. After the overthrow of the Shah, the clergy took charge. They used the CIA’s files to decimate the Tudeh and uproot the MeK. Given these proven propensities, would Dipke’s worldview remain true to the promise of the dreams Bhagat Singh and Ambedkar dreamt for India?
The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi.

title: No more torture
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
EVEN the best laws on the books are worth little unless the state shows the willingness to enforce them. This is certainly true for the Torture and Custodial Death (Prevention and Punishment) Act, 2022. As the HRCP pointed out during a recent consultation in Islamabad, torture and cruel and inhuman treatment remain widespread in Pakistan, despite the existence of this law. Perhaps the main reason for this is the thana culture that, despite multiple attempts at reform, continues to influence law enforcement in the country. This culture is a holdover from the colonial age during which LEAs were not supposed to serve and protect citizens, but to dominate them and put them in their place when they stepped out of line. The result is the continuation of a system where torture is endemic and rights are trampled on. Studies show that most confessions are extracted under torture. However, these brutish methods have failed to bring down crime numbers, as the rampant lawlessness across the country shows. The FIA told the Lahore High Court earlier this year that up till April 30, it had registered at least 364 inquiries under the anti-torture law. The vast majority of cases were reported from Punjab.
As speakers at the HRCP event noted, torture persists because of weak implementation, inadequate safeguards and a lack of accountability. At the root of the matter lies the need to revamp the criminal justice system. From police to prosecution, there is a need to sensitise public servants about fundamental rights, and replace archaic, violent and illegal methods with scientific techniques of investigation. The judiciary, elected representatives and the police hierarchy across the provinces must work together to reform the criminal justice system. This is imperative not because donors want reforms, but because the dignity of man, as underscored by the Constitution, must be upheld.
Published in Dawn, August 3rd, 2026

title: Farewell to arms?
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PALESTINIAN resistance group Hamas recently made a major concession by agreeing to give up its weapons. It should be remembered that along with its political activities, the movement has an armed wing dedicated to the liberation of Palestine. The group’s weapons will be surrendered to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, the Palestinian technocratic body formed under US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. In essence, Hamas has thrown the gauntlet to Israel: it is ready to surrender its weapons, but will the Zionist state end its occupation of Gaza? This remains the million-dollar question. Mr Trump was upbeat about the development, saying that Israel was “very happy” about it. However, while there had been no official reaction from Tel Aviv at the time of writing, most Israeli politicians, including some in the cabinet, have decried the move, calling for the destruction of Hamas.
It will be interesting to see whether Israel honours its end of the deal and vacates occupied Palestinian territory in Gaza. Going by past precedent, the Israelis are not known for keeping their word. Also, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces an election in October, and there is widespread anti-Palestinian sentiment amongst the electorate. But the Israeli leader may not want to annoy the American president by appearing to sabotage Mr Trump’s Gaza peace plan. Lest we forget, Israel has murdered over 73,000 Palestinians — more than 21,000 of them children — since the Oct 7, 2023 attacks, and while its killing spree has lessened in intensity, it has not stopped completely since the ceasefire came into effect last year. Moreover, the humanitarian situation in Gaza remains appalling. 
It should be kept in mind that Hamas and other Palestinian groups have continued their armed struggle against Israel because the Zionist state has closed all avenues of peacefully resolving the Palestine question. Almost the entire Israeli political class is opposed to a Palestinian state, illegal settlements continue to proliferate, and Gaza — which even before the 2023 attacks was virtually under siege — lies in ruins. Meanwhile, Israeli provocations against Al Aqsa have not stopped. If this situation is to change, there must be a clear pathway for a Palestinian state, an end to Israeli brutalities against the Arab population, and complete withdrawal from all occupied territories. Knowing the current political climate in Israel, this is asking for the moon. However, Mr Trump, who sees himself as a ‘peacemaker’, and his BoP must press Israel to at least start the process by withdrawing from Gaza, and allowing unimpeded humanitarian assistance into the Strip. If Tel Aviv does not leave Gaza, it will show the world that it is not serious about peace, and is committed to the occupation of Palestine and to the extermination of the Palestinian people.
Published in Dawn, August 3rd, 2026

title: Pakistan needs more provinces and strong local governments
author: Webdesk
content:
Throughout the world, successful federations have consistently recognised that as populations grow and economies become more complex, governments must move closer to the people. Decentralisation has become one of the defining features of effective governance. Nations that have periodically reorganised their administrative structures have generally experienced faster economic growth, better public services, stronger institutions and greater political stability.

The discussion on creating new provinces in Pakistan has unfortunately remained trapped within political and ethnic narratives. Such an approach obscures the real issue. Administrative reorganisation should never be viewed as a concession to regional politics; rather, it should be regarded as a constitutional instrument for improving governance and ensuring equitable development. Provinces should neither be created nor opposed on ethnic, linguistic or political grounds. Instead, objective criteria such as population, geographical size, administrative workload, accessibility, economic viability, infrastructure needs and national security should guide the process.

No major country has achieved sustained economic growth, administrative efficiency or political stability through excessive centralisation. Successful nations continuously adapt their administrative structures to changing demographic, economic and security realities. Administrative reform is therefore not an event but a continuous national process.

Pakistan, unfortunately, has moved in the opposite direction. Provincial governments have become increasingly centralised, while local governments remain financially weak and administratively dependent. Decision-making is concentrated in provincial capitals, leaving remote districts with limited influence over development priorities. The result has been uneven infrastructure development, delayed public services, weak municipal administration, inadequate policing and growing perceptions of regional inequality. These are not failures of democracy; they are failures of administrative design.

The solution lies not merely in creating additional provinces but in adopting a comprehensive national policy of decentralisation based upon constitutional principles, objective benchmarks and international best practices. Pakistan requires an administrative structure that is dynamic, evidence-based and capable of evolving with future demographic and economic changes rather than remaining frozen in the institutional framework of the past. Administrative reorganisation must be guided by objective constitutional principles rather than political expediency or ethnic considerations. A modern federation should periodically review its administrative structure to ensure that governance keeps pace with changing demographic, economic and security realities.

Pakistan therefore needs a permanent institutional mechanism to undertake this responsibility. Parliament should establish a National Commission on Administrative Reforms and Decentralisation through an Act of Parliament. The Commission should comprise constitutional experts, economists, public administration specialists, demographers, finance experts, urban planners, representatives of the armed forces and law enforcement agencies, members of the Planning Commission and representatives of all federating units. It should function as an independent constitutional policy body, reviewing Pakistan's administrative structure after every national census and recommending reforms based upon objective benchmarks rather than political pressures.

The Commission should establish measurable national standards, including population size, geographical area, administrative workload, distance from the provincial capital, accessibility of public services, economic sustainability, infrastructure requirements, law and order considerations, disaster management capacity, human development indicators and future population growth. Such an evidence-based approach would depoliticise the debate and ensure that administrative reforms serve the national interest rather than partisan interests.

One of the most important constitutional reforms requiring serious national discussion is the amendment of Article 239 of the Constitution. Under the existing constitutional framework, altering provincial boundaries is an extremely difficult process. While these constitutional safeguards were intended to protect the federating units, they have also made necessary administrative reforms almost impossible. Pakistan should therefore consider a constitutional amendment providing that, after laying down clear constitutional principles and safeguards, the establishment, merger or reorganisation of provinces may be undertaken by Parliament through an Act passed by a simple majority on the recommendations of the National Commission. Such a reform would enable the federation to respond to changing administrative realities through democratic parliamentary decision-making.

Administrative reforms should not stop at the provincial level. The greatest weakness in Pakistan's governance structure lies in the persistent neglect of local governments. Although Article 140A of the Constitution requires elected local governments with political, administrative and financial responsibility, this constitutional vision has never been fully realised.

No country has achieved efficient governance without empowering local governments. Pakistan must adopt a new model of fiscal decentralisation. Financial devolution should accompany administrative devolution. Local governments should receive predictable and constitutionally protected transfers under a transparent statutory formula linked to population, area, poverty levels, infrastructure deficits and development needs. District governments, metropolitan corporations, municipal committees and village councils should be empowered to plan and implement education, primary healthcare, sanitation, water supply, waste management, local roads, urban transport, housing regulation, parks, environmental protection and community development.

Administrative reorganisation should also become a continuous constitutional process rather than a one-time political exercise. After every national census, the proposed National Commission should assess whether existing provinces, divisions, districts and local governments continue to meet national benchmarks. Where necessary, Parliament should be empowered to undertake further administrative restructuring in accordance with objective constitutional criteria. Such a dynamic system would ensure that Pakistan's administrative architecture evolves alongside demographic and economic changes.

Pakistan's founders envisioned a federation founded upon justice, participation and efficient administration. Those constitutional aspirations require constant institutional renewal. The challenges of the 21st century cannot be addressed through administrative arrangements inherited from another era. Governance must evolve with the needs of the people. The real strength of a federation lies not in concentrating power but in distributing authority wisely, ensuring that every citizen enjoys equal access to public institutions and equal opportunities for development.

Administrative reorganisation, including the creation of new provinces, should be guided by objective criteria such as population, geographical size, and economic viability, rather than political expediency or ethnic narratives.

A comprehensive national policy of continuous decentralisation is required, involving a National Commission on Administrative Reforms, constitutional amendments (e.g., Article 239, 140A), and fiscal devolution to empower local governments at all levels.

title: Water coercion
author: none@none.com (Aizaz Ahmad Chaudhry)
content:
THAT India decided to suspend the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) 65 years after its signing has added another polemic to the turbulent relations between India and Pakistan. India’s decision came a day after the Pahalgam terrorist incident in India-occupied Kashmir. India blamed the incident on Pakistan, which demanded evidence and called for an independent investigation. Two days after the incident, the Indian minister for water resources, C.R. Patil, threatened that “not a single drop” of water would flow towards Pakistan. Ironically, while India cries foul, it is working actively to perpetuate proxy terrorism in Pakistan through the TTP and BLA.
The Narendra Modi government regards the IWT as historical injustice to India. Speaking to the Indian parliament in July 2025, Prime Minister Modi stated that holding the IWT in abeyance has rectified a “big blunder” committed by Jawaharlal Nehru. The argument is that the IWT gave Pakistan nearly 80 per cent of the Indus river system’s flows. Modi argued that India derived its identity from the Indus, but that Nehru and the Congress had allowed the World Bank to decide on the sharing of its waters. India’s leadership conveniently overlooks the fact that India receives 100pc of the waters of the three eastern rivers and is legally permitted to use 20pc of the water of the western rivers for irrigation, power generation and transport.
Indian thought circles are now weaving a narrative based on three elements: (i) IWT was an unequal bargain that must now be rectified; (ii) Pakistan’s insistence on treaty procedures was an impediment to India’s development projects that could benefit Kashmiris; (iii) Indian projects on the western rivers would not use more than the treaty-permitted 3.6 MAF (this cannot be verified as India is withholding information and has made the Indus Water Commission dysfunctional); and (iv) IWT should be renegotiated to account for demographic and environmental changes that have occurred since 1960.
This narrative is designed to take the international community’s attention away from India’s violation of international law as the IWT’s unilateral suspension isn’t allowed by the treaty. Besides, usurping the water rights of the lower riparian goes against the established norms of water sharing. Behind the façade of this narrative, India has started work on multiple dams, mostly on the Chenab river, and inter-basin transfers such as Chenab-Beas tunnel.
India can manipulate flows to hurt the sowing season in Pakistan.
Pakistan’s canal system works on the basis of predictable water flows. Given that India is building several dams and is not providing timely information, even a temporary reduction in flows during the sowing season can have a disastrous effect on Pakistan’s agriculture. That is why Pakistan is so concerned about Indian attempts to build these dams along with withholding information on water flows.
So, what options does Pakistan have to ensure its water security? An obvious one is to increase its diplomatic outreach so that the world understands that not only do India’s actions violate its legal obligations, they also threaten the lives and livelihoods of millions of Pakistanis dependent on the waters of the Indus basin. However, since the world order is in disarray and the prevailing global geopolitics is chaotic, India doesn’t seem to care much for diplomatic pressure. Legally, Pakistan’s case has been endorsed by the Hague-based Court of Arbitration, which has ruled that India’s attempt to place the IWT in abeyance has no legal basis and that India must ensure the uninterrupted flow of the western rivers. How­e­ver, India blata­n­tly rej­ected the awards. That bri­ngs into play the military option. Wars are a costly business, pa­­-r­ticularly bet­ween two nuclear-arm­­ed neighbo­urs. India needs to know that it must not test Pa­-kistan’s patience lest both countries end up in a disastrous situation.
Some experts say that India will not be able to steal more water because of the limitations of the hilly terrain, particularly in the case of the Indus. If it could have stolen, it would have certainly done so in the past 65 years. However, this view does not take into account regional geopolitics, which has driven India’s decision to suspend the treaty. While it is true that geography will not permit India to stop Pakistan’s share of water, it can manipulate flows to hurt the sowing season in the country. A dedicated Pakistan-India backchannel is necessary to resolve the deadlock before disaster strikes. In a package approach, India could restore the treaty while Pakistan accepts the negotiation of an addendum to the IWT on demographic and environmental changes. Pakistan should also work harder towards more efficient use of the water it receives and bolster its storage capacity.
The writer is chairman, Sanober Institute, and former foreign secretary of Pakistan.

title: Rethinking the auto policy
author: none@none.com (Ehsan Malik)
content:
PAKISTAN’S automobile industry captures the country’s industrial policy dilemma well. As the government considers lower tariffs, manufacturers warn of plant closures, job losses and wasted investment. Critics argue that, despite more than 40 years of protection, consumers until recently faced high prices and limited choice, while exports remained negligible.
Both sides have a point. But the debate is framed wrongly. The question is: can the country’s auto industry build capabilities that can compete in regional and global value chains?
One principle should guide policy. Except in strategically important sectors, any industry seeking protection must offer consumers better value and move towards international competitiveness. Protection should be a runway, not a refuge.
    
The auto industry deserves credit. It has built assemblers and component suppliers, developed engineering skills, invested in vendors and created skilled jobs despite expensive energy, costly finance, policy uncertainty, cumbersome regulation and weak logistics. But the main goals — saving foreign exchange through localisation and creating large-scale employment — were flawed from the start.
Can Pakistan’s auto industry build capabilities that can compete in regional and global value chains?
The first misconception was localisation. Auto policy assumed that making more components at home would ease pressure on the external account. That ignored how modern vehicles are made. Engines, transmissions, fuel injection systems, electronic controls and software carry much of a vehicle’s value. Producing them competitively requires deep upstream capacity in automotive-grade steel, petrochemicals, specialised alloys, precision engineering and electronics. Pakistan never built those foundations at scale, so localisation became a numerical target rather than a measure of real competitiveness.
Localisation numbers are also misleading. They count components assembled domestically, not domestic value added. Seats, batteries, tyres, wiring harnesses, glass, plastic mouldings and metal stampings may be made locally, but many depend on imported inputs and moulds and use energy generated from imported fuels. A 50 to 60 percent localisation rate can therefore produce far smaller foreign exchange savings than advertised. Better metrics would track net domestic value addition, foreign exchange displacement and exports of locally manufactured components.
The second misconception was jobs. Automobile manufacturing is capital-intensive. It relies heavily on automation because quality and precision leave little room for manual shortcuts. Pakistan’s largest assembler employs fewer than 2,500 people directly, and the three largest together less than 6,000. Suppliers add jobs, but the direct workforce remains small relative to the protection received. Dealerships, distribution and repair facilities would exist even if vehicles were imported fully built.
The third misconception was scale. Competitive automobile manufacturing depends on large volumes that spread fixed costs across millions of vehicles. Pakistan’s market, at fewer than 300,000 vehicles a year, is too small to support that model on its own. Policy made matters worse by treating motor vehicles as luxury goods and taxing demand down. One arm of government protected local assembly while another choked the scale needed to make it efficient. The domestic consumer paid for both.
None of this negates the industry’s achievements. It shows that policy was flawed and measured success against goals the industry’s structure made difficult, and at times impossible, to meet. Technology has now made the old debate even less useful. The global industry is moving from internal combustion engines to hybrids and EVs, changing where value is created. EVs eliminate or simplify many components around which Pakistan’s localisation strategy has traditionally been built. Engines, multi-speed gearboxes, exhaust systems, catalytic converters and fuel injection technologies become less important. Value shifts instead to batteries, electric motors, power electronics, battery management systems, semiconductors, sensors and software.
Pakistan must stop designing industrial policy around yesterday’s technologies. Hybrids are the practical bridge: they cut fuel use and emissions without depending on charging infrastructure or an electricity network not yet ready for mass EV adoption. The policy goal should no longer be higher localisation percentages. It should be higher domestic value addition, exports, lower environmental impact and deeper technological capability. Incentives should favour battery assembly, electric motors, power electronics, charging equipment, automotive software, precision engineering and advanced manufacturing. Pakistan’s IT sector can support connected vehicles, while commercially viable minerals should feed domestic battery material and mobility supply chains rather than leave the country with minimal processing.
    
Pakistan should position itself as a base for export-oriented investment, especially for Chinese EV producers looking to diversify production and reach regional markets. This will require predictable policy, competitive energy, efficient logistics, easier access to imported inputs and trade agreements that open real market access. Morocco shows what scale and access can achieve — it exports about 500,000 of the 600,000 vehicles it produces to the EU.
Successful automotive producers offer clear lessons. Japan, South Korea, China and Thailand supported their auto industries, but protection was temporary, conditional and tied to exports, productivity, technology transfer and upgrading. India built its auto sector behind restrictions on consumer choice, while Asean and Mercosur countries used regional production networks to achieve scale. Pakistan should draw from these experiences, but it cannot simply replicate them as its domestic market is too small, regional integration is weak and the technology frontier has moved on.
Tariffs in Pakistan should fall through a transparent, predictable schedule that gives firms time to adjust but no excuse to stand still. Government must lower economy-wide costs through energy, logistics and tax reform, while linking any remaining incentives to exports, domestic value addition, engineering depth and high-value hybrid and EV technologies — not production volumes or headline localisation rates.
The real choice is not protection or liberalisation. It is whether Pakistan keeps measuring success by yesterday’s metrics or prepares for tomorrow’s automotive industry. The next auto policy should reward value addition, exports, innovation and technological transformation, and not permanence behind tariff walls. That would serve manufacturers, consumers and competitiveness far better than another decade of sterile debate.
The writer is a former CEO of Unilever Pakistan and of the Pakistan Business Council.
Published in Dawn, August 2nd, 2026

title: American crisis
author: none@none.com (Huma Yusuf)
content:
THE Middle East is broiling. The US-Iran conflict is spilling across borders to Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Yemen, Iraq and various Gulf countries. For now, most eyes are on Saudi Arabia, which finds itself drawn into a conflict it was seeking to keep at its periphery. Riyadh last week joined Washington to target the Iran-backed Popular Mobilisation Forces in Iraq. This followed Saudi strikes against Houthi forces in Yemen in response to the targeting of Saudi oil tankers using Red Sea shipping routes. Experts anticipate Riyadh will launch a wider offensive against the Houthis over the coming days.
This risks turning what began as a US and Israeli effort against Iran into a region-wide conflict with sectarian contours. Forget US President Donald Trump’s February boast that the war would be over within weeks — security analysts now predict an up-to-a-decade-long conflagration.
Pakistan will find itself sucked into this quagmire with each development. Its mutual defence pact with the kingdom has been supplemented by participation in the newly formed maritime defence alliance, which aims to secure shipping routes in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden — critical alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz. Pakistan has vested interests in securing these routes — disruptions to oil trading have led to soaring oil prices and a nearly five per cent decrease in Saudi Arabia’s GDP in the last quarter, a fact highly relevant to nations that frequently depend on the kingdom’s largesse.
While the focus remains on each new front line in the conflict, the question that should be asked is why this war is continuing. Think back to a few weeks ago, when it seemed that the worst had to be over, given that Trump was tiring of the strategic miscalculation with Iran and looking ahead to a summer of fun: a visit from the British king, the football World Cup. No one expected the conflict to drag into the autumn, thereby risking Trump’s party’s position in the US mid-term elections in November.
One in four of those who voted for Trump in 2024 opposes the war.
The electoral run-up, in particular, defies Trump’s logic of ramping up the Iran conflict. One in four of those who voted for Trump in 2024 opposes the war. Many MAGA supporters, with Tucker Carlson among the most vocal, believe the conflict is misaligned with the movement’s ‘America First’ isolationist principles.
Non-MAGA Republicans and the independents whom Trump won over in droves in the last election also find the conflict to be a turn-off. An AP-NORC poll conducted between July 23–27 in the US found that 64pc of Americans do not believe the war with Iran is worth fighting. More detailed surveys conducted in May by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs highlighted that 86pc of Americans are concerned about the war’s impact on the cost of living, 72pc believe it is damaging to the country’s overseas reputation and foreign relations, and 65pc believe it undermines the country’s national security — arguably the most damning finding given that Trump’s original war justifications focused on securing the US and its allies against overstated Iranian aggression.
US public opinion of Trump and his ill-conceived war is likely to worsen as the conflict escalates and midterms approach. In June 2026, consumer costs were almost 4pc higher than a year ago, with American truckers paying more for fuel and American farmers paying more for fertilisers. Cash-strapped Americans will not be pleased to hear that the Pentagon requires $80 billion more to continue fighting, having already spent $37.5bn to date.
So why are we here? Security analysts believe Trump thinks that military might yet get the better of the Iranians, either through military control of the Str­ait of Hormuz or through the dep­loyment of grou­­nd troops in Iran — an option previously conside­r­­ed a red line but now increasingly discussed as an endgame prospe­­ct. This perception of a military solution is fuelled by the gains experienced by America’s military economy, which is growing at the expense of other domestic investment, including investment in public services.
But the true driver of this prolonged conflict is more existential, as the US grapples with its place in a shifting world order, balancing a desire for global influence against a growing need for internal sociopolitical and economic consolidation. Khalid Al Jaber, writing for the Middle East Council, summarised it well: “The Iranian crisis revealed that Washington’s deepest challenge lies not on the battlefield … but in managing an internally deepening division between two competing and contradictory visions for the future of America’s global role: the leadership-through-strength or ‘America First’ vision … and the domestic rebalancing vision.” Multipolarity is real, but we still inhabit a world where America’s existential crisis is the world’s problem. 
The writer is a political and integrity risk analyst.

title: Damage assessment
author: none@none.com (Maleeha Lodhi)
content:
PRESIDENT Donald Trump’s approval rating has hit an all-time low according to the latest Economist/YouGov poll. The survey found 62 per cent of Americans disapprove of the president’s performance while 63pc say the country is headed in the wrong direction. These are Trump’s worst numbers since he returned to the White House last year. The results align with findings of other polls, which show he has fallen out of favour with the majority of Americans. The slide isn’t just about an unpopular war with Iran. Trump’s management of the economy is also driving public discontent. 
The first 18 months of the mercurial leader’s second term have been defined by disruption at home and abroad. His ‘America First’ unilateralism has meant military strikes on multiple countries and upending of the global trading system. It reflects contempt for international law and other nations’ sovereignty. For a president who promised to end wars, not start them, his record is the opposite. Trump assumed American power could browbeat other countries into compliance at no cost to the US. That was a miscalculation. His overreliance on force also failed to produce the results he wanted. 
Trump may be extreme in his imperious, unilateralist ways but there is continuity with past US conduct in an important respect. Throughout its history of dealing with other nations, the US has underestimated the power of nationalism and the resistance it would meet in trying to force its will on others. It found that in its interventions in Vietnam, Afghanistan and Iraq, which entangled Washington in unwinnable wars, produced strategic blunders and doomed its military adventures. Today, it is finding that again in the war against Iran. Trump also doesn’t seem to understand that the unipolar world long passed into history. In today’s multipolar world, countries will not so easily bend to Washington’s will. Indeed, the more Trump makes blusterous claims and tweets about how he has the power to get what he wants, the more it exposes his inability to secure his goals.
There is no shortage of commentary on Donald Trump’s personality and record. Two of the latest books are worth noting. Regime Change by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan and Betrayed: America didn’t vote for this by Ira Shapiro and Anne Kim. Both cover the first year plus of Trump’s second presidency and deliver stinging indictments of his performance. Betrayed is written by a broad coalition of distinguished bipartisan experts from among former government officials, lawyers, scholars and journalists. They are members of what is called the Common Sense Coalition. They chronicle the damage Trump has done to his country and to America’s standing in the world. This damage assessment is undertaken across multiple areas — economy, foreign policy, democracy and free speech, judiciary, voting system, education and climate. The book’s main point is that Americans did not vote for what Trump is doing and the disorder he is producing. His abuses of power must be stopped and his team members held accountable if America’s crisis is to end.
With his approval ratings having plunged Trump’s conduct has hardened global attitudes towards the US.
Though brief the chapters are pointed. The one on a weaker America is especially sharp. It argues that Trump has fractured the foundations for global stability. His costly and impetuous military adventures without a strategy or respect for international law and his contempt for traditional allies have endangered US security. The authors describe an unchecked president dragging the country into multiple conflicts with scant regard for the fallout. The attack on Iran, they argue, lays bare the hallmarks of his foreign policy decision making — impulsiveness, prioritising force over diplomacy, failure to take rational decisions based on their likely impact and trashing the concerns of allies. They frame his National Security Strategy as a reversal of eight decades of US foreign policy. 
This has resulted in ‘America Weaker’ and ‘America Alone’ and drained its soft power. Its international stature has diminished. Trump has alienated virtually all allies who had helped the US maintain global peace. The authors also argue Trump has misused and politicised the military and packed it with yes-men afraid of telling him the truth. 
In the chapter on the rule of law the writers hold Trump guilty of violating limits on presidential power, threatening the integrity of courts and usurping Congressional powers. Core civil liberties have been threatened. He is seen as weaponising government machinery including the Justice Department to punish political opponents and suppress dissent. He has violated court orders and vilified judges while shielding his friends from legal accountability. 
Regime Change is no less scathing about Trump’s record in office. Its subtitle Inside the imperial presidency of Donald Trump indicates its focus is on the inner workings of the White House. It is a riveting, richly sourced account of the chaos wreaked by a president who has acted with impunity and radically changed the office he occupies. It narrates how efforts have been made to stop Trump but failed. Based on over 1,000 interviews, it takes the readers behind the scenes to offer insights into Trump’s decision-making that has been so consequential and of course harmful for the country. 
How his team fell in line with his decisions even when they strongly disagreed is exemplified by a telling exchange between Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu during his February visit to Washington when he convinced Trump to attack Iran. The Israeli leader assured Trump that regime change would succeed in Iran and its nuclear capability would be destroyed, before Tehran could seize the Strait of Hormuz. The CIA director rubbished this view while the secretary of state called it “farcical”. But Trump prevailed.
Trump’s conduct has hardened global attitudes toward the US. Friends, allies and adversaries view the erratic swings in American policy with alarm. The latest poll by the Pew Research Centre captures the shift. China is viewed more favourably than the US in most countries surveyed. Given the turbulence of the past 18 months, that result is hardly unexpected. 
The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.
Published in Dawn, August 3rd, 2026

title: A hard state?
author: none@none.com (Umair Javed)
content:
THESE days we are repeatedly told that the Pakistani state has been soft on anarchy for far too long. This is the considered and stated position of many state officials as well as of many supporters of those in power. Common people may hold any number of positions that one finds distasteful but the same sentiments being voiced by those in power invite both scrutiny and concern.
For the last three years, there has been much chatter about turning Pakistan into a ‘hard state’. No one has given an adequate definition of what this entails, but based on disparate statements and impulses, we can gather this has something to do with protecting the rights of the state and the decision-makers who staff it. These rights are being obtained via a frequently violent trade-off with the rights of the people of Pakistan. 
The projected consequence of such a trade-off is that protest of all shades becomes a privilege. Demands can only be voiced with due approval through vetted content and NOCs. Speech is to be regulated via defamation, criminalisation laws, and an apparently pliant judiciary till it takes on an acceptable hue, or preferably till it becomes an echo of the state’s.
These impulses are neither unique to the Pakistani state nor are they exceptional to this current moment. Trysts with authoritarianism dot the country’s past and arguably lie at the roots of its state structure. British viceregal authority bequeathed an overdeveloped administrative apparatus, which has since then done exceedingly well to reproduce itself and the privileges of those who staff it. When given a chance, politicians of nearly all stripes — centralists, federalists, provincial magnates, or constituency-level bigwigs — have been more than happy to fortify this arrangement for their own and their clients’ benefits.
And yet there is a question that should gnaw at anyone who thinks about the trade-off at the table. What is all of this for? If people are being asked to voluntarily or otherwise forfeit their constitutional or social rights, it only makes sense to interrogate what end goal this forfeiture is designed to serve.
Beyond the protection of geographic boundaries, what other objectives do limits on individual liberty serve?
Forfeiture of individual liberty is commanded by all states in service of some basic objectives. Usually the foremost of these objectives is territorial sanctity: no state tolerates geographic loss and will usually strip people of their rights, property and lives to prevent it. The Pakistani state is fairly typical in this manner. It deals with separatism/secessionism the way many other post-colonial states do, and with variable degrees of success. The bigger question on that front then is whether its strategy for preventing the rise or growth of this factor is useful at all.
Beyond the protection of geographic boundaries, what other objectives do limits on individual liberty serve? Other states offer different types of answers. The case of China — paradigmatic for the 21st century — has a very simple one. It places limits on various forms of individual rights for the protection and promotion of the CCP’s endeavours. The main endeavour, since the 1970s at least, has been the growth and collective prosperity of the Chinese people via the unleashing of productive forces (labour and capital), both by the state and by private enterprise. The state under one-party rule decides the degree of this unleashing, its objectives, and ultimately the distribution of its fruits.
In the previous century, socialist states decided that the true fulfilment of human life lay in getting rid of privatised forms of exploitation. And so a suspension of individual liberty was done in service of collective ownership of resources, commandeered by the state. Social democratic states in Western Europe decided to infringe on the rights of capital owners over their profit in order to redistribute benefits to the working class via taxation. The late-20th-century Asian Tigers took away social rights of the working poor to generate double-digit capitalist growth.
There are other, less palatable answers too. The fascists in Germany stripped the rights, property, and lives of one minority group and various ideological dissenters (primarily the communists) in service of its ethnonationalist and expansionist agenda. At present, the ruling party in India targets individual liberties of specific segments, such as Muslims, to fulfil the cultural agenda of its majority base.
In all of these examples, the use of state power is for some larger agenda; a larger agenda in the name of the public (or at least an important part of it), built on specific ideational values and postulates. Something being done in service of something bigger, grander, and to varying degrees, collective.
So one must pose the question: what objective does this particular, three-year-old vintage of the ‘hard state’ serve in Pakistan?
To date there is no coherent answer. We do not know what the killing of protesters — regardless of the agreeability of their demands — in AJK is going to achieve. What goal banning political movements in the peripheries serves. What Form-47ing election outcomes does. What the hollowing out of the opposition, judiciary, media or civil society helps obtain.
If the answer is to maintain territorial integrity, then the vast majority of those whose rights stand stripped away carry no geographic ambitions. If the answer is to unleash GDP growth rates of the kind unseen in the last two decades, then one must reluctantly point out that the needle is yet to move up at all. If the answer is to project sovereignty and stature on the world stage at a time of global upheaval, the logical follow-up is a) whose stature and b) sovereignty in whose name?
There are no ready grand answers at the end of this line of inquiry because there is likely no grand thought among those steering the ‘hardening’. The actual answers, if one were to hazard a guess, are probably several degrees more modest: the prolonging of duration in office, an improvement in personal quality of life, and the distribution of gifts and sinecures to a small coterie of loyalists at the expense of everyone else. 
The writer teaches politics and sociology at Lums.

title: Urban flooding
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE warning from the disaster management and weather authorities that a new monsoon spell could trigger urban flooding in major cities across Punjab and Sindh is yet another reminder of how poorly prepared our cities are for heavy rainfall.
Cities from Rawalpindi, Lahore and Multan in Punjab, to Hyderabad, Umerkot and Tando Allahyar in Sindh, have been flagged for urban flooding. This is not unusual during the monsoons. However, what makes this year’s warning worth pausing on is the Met Office’s forecast of below normal rainfall this year. Still, less rainfall will not eliminate the risk of flooded cities if a burst of rain arrives faster than the ground and drains can carry it away. This says more about the state of our cities than about the weather.
The problem of urban flooding in Pakistan is no longer limited to low-lying neighbourhoods. It has become a structural feature of how the country has grown and urban centres have developed. Unplanned construction has taken place over drainage channels and wetlands that once absorbed rain. Waterways have been encroached upon, storm-water systems are built for outdated rainfall patterns, and drains are choked with solid waste that no longer has any place to go.
    
The response is reactive across the provinces. Drains are cleared only when the rain starts to fall; pumps arrive after roads are under water; and warnings are issued, repeated, then forgotten until the next spell. This is crisis management dressed up as preparedness. Most Pakistani cities have no comprehensive flood-risk maps, no functioning drainage master plans, and no clear chain of command for who acts first as the water rises. Drainage, roads, water supply and disaster response sit in separate departments that rarely coordinate before a flood and mostly trade blame after one.
Climate change has broken the old planning assumptions. Cities now need infrastructure built for short, intense downpours capable of overwhelming drains within minutes, not the gradual rainfall patterns those systems were designed around decades ago. Every new road, housing scheme or commercial project should be assessed for how it disrupts the natural water flow before approval, not after the damage becomes visible. Existing drains need redesigning and expanding to match current rainfall intensity, rather than being patched up just before the monsoon.
    
Pakistan cannot control how much rain falls. But it can control the extent to which the rain turns into a disaster. The recent warning is not a new problem; each year, governments assure the public that they are ready for the rains. Unfortunately, the very first intense downpour exposes their claims. What the country needs is sustained investment in drainage infrastructure and local governments to maintain it between the monsoons, not just during the rainy season.

title: Power and youth
author: none@none.com (Muhammad Amir Rana)
content:
YOUTH are highly innovative in expressing their anger. Meanwhile, ruling elites struggle to understand that the existing power structure can no longer meet the aspirations of the young. The context of this statement is neither the events in Delhi, where the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) succeeded in achieving its demands, nor the violent protests in Azad Jammu and Kashmir, nor the recent provocative statement by the federal interior minister about the state system. Rather, the reference is to a silent protest by the youth of Khuzdar in Balochistan, in which they succeeded in having their demand met. Is it not a unique event in Pakistan when the demands of the youth are met?
What was the youth’s demand? The reopening of a local library, where students study and prepare for their civil service examinations. The library was closed by the local bureaucracy, quite likely with the consent of superior institutions, which see books and libraries as sources of dissent. One cannot spare the bureaucracy either, which has a narrow vision and has been taught to rule like colonial masters. There is a high probability that in Khuzdar, too, they would have seen the youth’s inclination towards books and literature as a potential threat to security. It is ironic that most students, including many female students, were using the library as a safe and peaceful space to prepare for their exams. Most of them aspired to become bureaucrats, but the bureaucracy itself had shut down the library and closed the door to their future.
    
Whatever factors were involved in the library’s shutdown, the youth adopted a unique and peaceful way to protest. They held a sit-in outside the library and converted the footpaths and adjoining street into an open-air study space. They did not raise any slogans or attempt to confront the police or the local administration; they simply continued sitting silently and studying. Finally, the Balochistan chief minister intervened, and the library doors opened again.
This peaceful protest happened in a conflict-torn province where an insurgency is at its peak. The state has cracked down on violent actors. Sadly, those who participate in peaceful political and civil rights movements are also targeted. The district of Khuzdar has its own complex local, tribal and political context, and sardars, good or bad, have made the local people’s lives miserable. Yet the youth found a way to register their protest.
The youth are not politically blind; they see how the system works and how it is manoeuvred.
The protests by the youth in Khuzdar and by the CJP in India were related to education and inspired by the idea of getting a fair chance in life. Power structures have lost sight of the fact that equal opportunities and a fair system are essential for the youth. The youth are not politically blind; they see how the system works and how it is manoeuvred.
Whether it is referred to as Gen Z or Alpha-Z, this is a different generation with a different worldview. A dominant trend, especially among the more privileged youth of this generation, is to try out new modes of production and expand their class influence. Their forefathers accumulated leverage for their protection through wealth and relationships within the power structure. Less privileged youth are becoming less interested in civil services and industries and more interested in the corporate and financial sectors.
    
Certainly, the majority still belong to the middle- and lower-income groups, and they try every avenue they believe can empower them. They know that power is the only pathway to economic prosperity. Civil services and public-sector jobs of any sort are their shortcuts to finding a way out.
When someone tries to block the path to their dreams, they resist and protest. The older generations respond to the new generation in the conventional way, claiming that the new generation knows nothing. Where the youth have brought about political change, as in Nepal and Bangladesh, senior figures in the system dislike them and see their worldview as flawed.
A crisis is unfolding in Pakistan, particularly for the country’s youth. A draconian shift is taking place in the world of politics, where the older generation of politicians is transferring its legacy, power, and values to the next generation — not through legitimate constitutional and political means, but through shady deals with the most powerful. This process is occurring in every party, and the transition is frightening because those to whom power is being transferred have very little connection with political processes. They believe they are chosen to rule and can do anything to retain power. The youth of the country, then, has nothing to be proud of or to be inspired by in the existing political order.
This piece is not meant to predict any Gen Z-style uprising in Pakistan, but to point out that the political structure has become so tarnished and corrupt that it cannot sustain the burden of the economy, create new economic engines, or effectively utilise the existing sources of wealth. The bureaucratic structure is incapable of running governance and is becoming increasingly ruthless. A sense of deprivation is a common thread among young people from the middle- and lower-income classes.
Those in power are unwilling to review their practices; instead, they believe in an authoritarian, hegemonic style of controlling the system, in which subjects are expected to behave and follow whatever those in power dictate. The concept of citizenship was eroded long ago, and those who are powerless are treated merely as subjects. If they protest and their demands are fulfilled, they must consider themselves lucky, be thankful to the powerful, and forget that their success has anything to do with their ability to express themselves differently.
The writer is a security analyst.
Published in Dawn, August 2nd, 2026

title: Not the right questions
author: none@none.com (Ghazan Jamal)
content:
BUDGET season is behind us — and with it the opportunity for productive conversations and comparisons centring on inter-governmental development priorities and structural reforms. In recent memory, the only time such conversations flooded the airwaves was after the KP chief minister’s visits to Lahore and Karachi some months ago. For a brief moment, comparisons between the progress achieved under the PTI’s 12-year rule in KP and the track record of parties in other provinces dominated the political discourse — from street discussions among residents to heated arguments between party leaders on national programmes. Given the divisive political slurs that normally eclipse serious political discussions, the debate on actual governance and performance was indeed a welcome change. How­ever, that is where the positivity ended. While greater insight may elude the man on the street regarding service delivery and development, the questions and responses of policymakers, elected officials and senior anchorpersons leave much to be desired. This is particularly apparent during the budget season — in the days leading up to its announcement and immediately after the document is released. It was no different this year.
For example, discussions on the education sector’s performance tended to focus on the number of new university buildings inaugurated. Elementary and secondary education were too ‘unimportant’ to even mention. This is ironic, considering that the government is constitutionally mandated to provide education to every citizen from ages five to 16. One would have hoped to see greater commentary on important aspects such as the progress made on increasing literacy rates and reducing the number of out-of-school children, improving test scores, fund allocation at the primary and secondary levels, and university admissions. Rather than listen to long-winded discussions on expensive infrastructure development at the higher education level, one would have preferred detailed analyses on the total number of graduates and how many of them were absorbed into the labour force, academic research and publications, university affordability, the financial status of public universities and their national and international rankings. These are crucial factors; unfortunately, the performance of many public universities has worsened on these fronts. Discussions on the topic could have exposed the government’s lethargy and challenged policymakers to do better. 
To assess various parties’ records on healthcare, the debate took a similar track, with party spokespersons essentially focused on naming large or tertiary-level hospitals inaugurated during their tenure. Emphasising expensive, specialised care is a misguided and wasteful approach in a country where the overwhelming majority of preventable deaths are due to causes that are treatable at the basic healthcare facility level or through improvement in public health efforts. The latter include better sanitation and vaccination outreach as well as behavioural changes. In Pakistan’s context, focusing the discussion on plans to increase the number of hospital beds, doctors and paramedic staff, improve access to basic healthcare, and keep healthcare affordable would be a better yardstick for comparing provincial performances. What is also left out is key health data, such as trends in mortality, disease and infection rates, and immunisation coverage. In a country where over 40 per cent of children under the age of five are affected by stunting (a consequence of poor hygiene and malnourishment), it was disappointing not to have comparisons focus on improvements in WASH and nutrition.
Similarly, there was little discussion on countering inflation and poverty. A recent report on poverty rates presents a damning picture: poverty rates have been increasing in all the provinces over the last few years. The other key economic concern for citizens is unemployment. Again, conversations about government interventions to lessen unemployment or about provincial enterprises and industrial policies, or even about boosting growth in general, never really got off the ground. This exposes the disconnect between broadcasters and policymakers and the issues that most affect people’s lives. It would have been very instructive for the public to hear informed conversations about these issues as well.
In at least two of the provinces, KP and Balochistan, security has become one of the biggest concerns for the public. Yet the debate arou­­nd the issue has focused more on jurisdictional disputes rather than actual efforts to ensure security. It is true that both the federal and provincial governments have a role to play in maintaining security, but constitutionally policing is strictly a provincial subject. Yet, rather than discuss interventions that have improved or aim to improve policing through better training, prosecutorial success, community engagement, equipment upgradation and other programmes, the parties were only keen to deflect responsibility — with not enough pushback from the anchorpersons. 
A more honest political discourse focused on crucial issues is needed.
Worst of all, there has been little conversation about key legislation passed. Often, there is criticism that parliamentarians are more interested in development work than legislation; yet the legislative output of their respective parties, and how it determines their performance, is hardly discussed. Perhaps the only exception is the citing of the 18th Amendment by the PPP and ANP. While this may be seen as a joint accomplishment by the provinces, surely political representatives can be asked to explain the performance of their respective provincial government and how it measures up to the policies made or the laws passed. Indeed, the policies and laws themselves are a point of discussion to see how far they go in promoting (or restricting) democratic norms.
Pakistan’s political discourse will benefit from more evidence-based third-party evaluation of provincial governments’ performances across all sectors over the past couple of decades. This will not only help foster healthy competition between the parties and their governments, but, more importantly, it will create an atmosphere of cross-province learning and best practices. A more honest political discourse focused on the right issues among party spokespeople and policymakers would contribute greatly to the designing and implementation of programmes to make Pakistan more prosperous. The first step to inculcate such a constructive atmosphere begins by asking the right questions.
The writer is a development practitioner and a former parliamentarian.
