title: Invisible women
author: none@none.com (Dur e Sameen Akhund)
content:
PAKISTAN’S export economy runs on women’s work. Walk through a stitching unit in Faisalabad or a cotton field in southern Punjab and this is obvious. Yet open the audit reports, supplier scorecards and compliance files that govern access to our largest export markets and the women largely disappear: present in the aggregate headcount, absent from the wage data, the grievance logs, the risk assessments. For decades this invisibility was commercially convenient. It is now becoming a commercial liability.
The reason is a quiet shift in how our buyers are regulated. The European Union, which takes roughly a third of Pakistan’s exports under GSP-Plus preferences, adopted its Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive in 2024. Brussels narrowed its scope this March. Some have read that as a reprieve; it’s not: the companies still covered, above 5,000 employees and 1.5 billion in turnover, are precisely the brands ordering from Pakistan, and will comply by pushing questionnaires down the chain. The directive does not treat risk as gender-neutral. The OECD, whose framework underpins it, is blunt in a new case study on gender in supply chains: gendered harms are systemic, informal and often invisible, and due diligence that does not look for them will not find them.
A brand’s compliance team in Amsterdam reviews your file. Your audits show no findings on harassment, no discrimination, no gender pay gap because pay data was never disaggregated by sex. Ten years ago, that was a clean file. Today it invites a harder question. A nationally representative survey in Bangladesh found a third of women garment workers reporting workplace harassment. Pakistan has no equivalent figure; nobody has counted; that gap is the red flag. The Time Use Survey 2007showed women carrying roughly 11 times the unpaid care work of men. That imbalance decides who can accept overtime, who gets promoted and who ends up in the home-based operations that audits never reach. An audit that finds nothing is no longer proof of a clean operation. It is proof that nobody looked. Silence in the data has stopped being reassuring.
Pakistani industry has been slow to register this. Gender in the supply chain is still filed under corporate social responsibility. It has quietly become an order-book issue. The suppliers who retain European business will be those able to answer a buyer’s questionnaire with credible, sex-disaggregated evidence: who works where and on what contract, what women are paid relative to men, whether grievance channels are used by women. The suppliers who cannot will not be dropped for having problems; they will be dropped for being unable to show they know what their problems are. Under a due diligence regime, the unknowable supplier is the risky supplier.
Pakistan’s export sectors were built on the labour of women.
There is an opportunity here. Pakistan competes against Bangladesh, Vietnam and Cambodia, all facing the same tide; the first to equip its exporters to respond credibly gains an advantage no tariff schedule can provide. Some raw material exists: the Protection Against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, strengthened in 2022, and the Sindh Home-Based Workers Act 2018. At CERB, we have documented what happens when companies treat women’s inclusion as supply chain strategy rather than philanthropy. One of the country’s largest denim exporters, took its Cotton Initiative into the fields it sources from, training women farmers and building supplementary household incomes; the gains run from women’s earnings and decision-making power to the resilience of the company’s own cotton base. A companion study in dairy, Nou­­rishing Lives, tra­­ces the impact on emp­owering wom­en in milk supply chain. The­se are commercial firms strengthening supply chains they depend on.
The task divides naturally. Exp­or­t­ers should stop tre­ating the absence of complaints as an ach­ievement and start measuring what the new regimes ask about: pay, contract type and grievance uptake, broken down by sex. Industry associations should build shared tools, because a questionnaire answered well once can be ans­w­ered well a hundred times. And government, which lobbies Brussels hard for GSP-Plus renewal, must recognise that its strongest submission is not diplomatic but evidentiary — a demonstrable effort to make these women visible, counted and protected.
None of this requires solving deep structural inequality before the next order cycle. Due diligence regimes do not demand perfection; they demand honesty about risk and seriousness about addressing it. What they punish is blindness. Pakistan’s export sectors were built on the labour of women the system was designed not to see. The buyers can no longer afford that arrangement. Soon, neither can we. 
The writer is a senior manager sustainability at the Pakistan Business Council’s Centre of Excellence in Responsible Business.
Published in Dawn, July 29th, 2026

title: Still vulnerable
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE State Bank’s decision to hold the policy rate at 11.5pc is a prudent response to the heightened risks the economy faces on account of the renewed conflict in the Middle East. The economy has gained some measure of stability, but the foundations remain fragile. Inflation has moderated, but remains above the SBP target range of 5-7pc, even if the bank expects it to fall gradually, most likely near the upper limit, going forward. Foreign exchange reserves have improved, the external account is broadly manageable due to a consistent rise in remittances and economic activity is showing signs of modest recovery. Still, much of this stability remains vulnerable to external shocks and could quickly come under pressure from higher global commodity prices, rising input costs, food inflation, domestic energy prices adjustments and climate-related events. The Middle East crisis makes the risks particularly acute. Pakistan remains heavily dependent on imported energy. Any sustained surge in energy prices would further push up the import bill, intensify inflationary pressures and put pressure on the current account and currency. The relief provided by the earlier de-escalation could be reversed.
The bank’s decision to wait, therefore, reflects a sensible balancing act. A premature rate cut could fuel inflation and weaken external stability. But the monetary policy has its own limitations. On its own, it cannot insulate Pakistan from oil shocks, fix the tax system, reform the energy sector or raise productivity. That is where the government’s responsibility begins. The present stabilisation has been achieved at a considerable economic and social cost. It cannot become an end in itself. Heavy external financing requirements, debt repayments and continued dependence on refinancing mean that we remain exposed to shifts in global markets and geopolitical conditions. An improved sovereign credit rating and stronger reserves provide breathing space. But neither should be confused with economic security. The message of the policy rate decision is more important than the decision itself. The government must use this breathing space to address the structural weaknesses that have pushed Pakistan towards economic crises. The challenge is not just to protect stability but to turn it into sustainable growth by increasing exports, attracting investment and creating employment without landing the country into another balance-of-payments crisis.

title: Guarding the past
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE return of 513 smuggled archaeological artefacts from the US is a welcome homecoming for objects that should never have left Pakistan. That most belong to the Gandhara civilisation makes the recovery especially significant, given the region’s importance as a crossroads of Buddhist, Greek and Central Asian influences. Yet, the uncomfortable question remains: how were these treasures allowed to disappear in the first place? Repatriation, however valuable, is only the final piece of a puzzle that began with theft, weak protection and an illicit international market willing to profit from cultural plunder. The Senate committee is therefore right to demand a comprehensive account of the smuggling network, the value of the recovered relics and the fate of those still missing. While recovering heritage is commendable, preventing its loss is the greater obligation.
The proposed museum to display these artefacts will do well to strengthen public appreciation of Pakistan’s diverse civilisational inheritance. However, preservation requires far more than exhibition space. Archaeological sites remain vulnerable to encroachment, illegal excavation and poorly supervised development, as concerns over the reported demolition of a Mughal-era structure illustrate. Equally important is ensuring that conservation meets international standards. It is encouraging that Unesco’s reservations over restoration work at Taxila appear to have been addressed through adherence to recognised conservation principles. Maintaining that credibility matters if Pakistan wishes to secure inscription for more sites on the World Heritage List and expand cultural tourism. Technology, tighter border controls, specialised investigative units and closer international cooperation must become permanent features of the fight against antiquities trafficking. Protecting Pakistan’s inheritance demands sustained political commitment, professional stewardship and meaningful accountability. The recovery of these treasures is a victory, but ensuring that no more are lost would be the greater achievement.

title: Humbled by pests
author: none@none.com (Mahir Ali)
content:
HUMILITY isn’t a trait commonly associated with the Indian prime minister. Hence his education minister’s exit last weekend was greeted as a triumph by the crowds who had been demanding it for weeks, and acknowledged as an unusual retreat by analysts familiar with the Modi regime’s tendency to resist popular pressure.
In itself, Dharmendra Pradhan’s departure isn’t such a big deal even for a government that prides itself on avoiding ministerial resignations. He has been replaced by another Modi loyalist — RSS alumnus, Pralhad Joshi. Whether Joshi, who also holds other portfolios, is even inclined to redress the challenges in the educational sector is one among many questions.
The leak of questions in medical entrance exams in which 2.3 million aspirants were competing for fewer than 130,000 places necessitated a retake. At least 12 students died by suicide in the interim; several more are said to have died since then. The leaks are not uncommon: at least 152 are said to have occurred since 2014, when Narendra Modi became PM. As with other socioeconomic facets of India’s polity, such flaws were exacerbated rather than introduced by the BJP government that took over 12 years ago.
However, this regime cannot evade the charge that funding for the education ministry and support for the University Grants Commission has declined precipitously under its watch, or that almost 100,000 public schools have been shut. For students’ families, the average price of higher education has surged by over 90 per cent. Millions of parents mortgage or sell off what they own in a quest to educate their offspring. But even after some of those children obtain the necessary degrees, their job prospects often turn out to be dismal.
This is by no means exclusively an Indian issue. It has echoes throughout South Asia and the Global South, wherever a youth bulge collides with the unforgiving forces of neoliberal capitalism. However, India represents the world’s sixth largest economy, and aspires to ascend the ladder. The rage of the youth against barriers to advancement does not gel with that image.
This is by no means exclusively an Indian issue.
Delhi’s Jantar Mantar protesters were mollified by the concessions to their main demands, including no charges against the organisers. They protested largely peacefully, despite police provocations to thwart a march on parliament. They dispersed equally peacefully after their limited victories. The big question is what, if anything, comes next.
The rejoicing was well-deserved, but the most significant lesson from the unexpected upsurge is that it’s possible to push the regime to respond to popular pressure. Amid previous revolts, it has resorted to exacerbating sectarian, caste or ethnic divides in digging its way out of the hole. That turned out to be much harder when many of those out on the streets were middle-class Hindus whose parents in many cases had previously placed their faith in the BJP, but are now increasingly alarmed by its follies.
The consequences of this brief interlude in Indian politics remain clouded. It was an inspiring rebellion that sparked echoes not only across the nation but also among the diaspora in Europe and the Americas. And it was notable that among the mostly young rebels, differences of class, caste, faith and even ideology were at least temporarily obliterated. Abhijit Dipke, who instigated the revolt with a clever response to the Indian chief justice’s obnoxious remarks about unemployed ‘cockroaches’, has rightly noted that by ignoring the divisive efforts to provoke Hindu-Muslim or caste hostility, the issues that really matter can be directly targeted. And possibly resolved.
He and several other participants in the protests have also indicated that this is just the beginning. On Mon­day, the Cockroach Janta Party threatened to relaunch its protests after hundreds of arrests across BJP-ruled states in contravention of Saturday’s ceasefire. The Sangh Parivar has undoubtedly been rattled, given that quite a few protesters were motivated mainly by mounting distress at the hopeless direction in which Modi’s India has been headed. Some of the demonstrators indicated that they were sorely disappointed by the lack of support from cowardly Indian celebrities, barring respected stalwarts of the old guard such as Amol Palekar, Shabana Azmi and, above all, Naseeruddin Shah.
Speculating about India’s future or the effects of its recent predicament on neighbours is a mug’s game. But it’s worth recalling the student-led revolt that toppled Pakistan’s first military dictator almost six decades ago, paving the way for a short-lived democracy. That was a different time and place, but whatever comes next, the Delhi protests ought to be remembered by historians for inspiring hope at a time when the political opposition was floundering in the face of institutionalised fanaticism.

title: A water security policy
author: editorial
content:
Pakistan is trapped in an abusive relationship with the monsoon season, as the same rains that are crucial for farmers are death-bringers for people in flood-sensitive areas. The numbers are staggering: the 2022 floods submerged one-third of the country, affected 33 million people and caused over $30 billion in damages. The 2025 floods claimed 1,039 lives, displaced more than four million people and inflicted billions more in economic losses. We have also seen crippling floods this year, though fortunately not on the same scale. Still, many of these disasters could have been mitigated, or even largely avoided, if we had a comprehensive national water security policy.

Experts have long warned that Pakistan must move beyond short-term emergency responses and adopt a comprehensive water strategy to address growing flood risks and the worsening water crisis. Part of the problem is that, right now, while we do have policies relating to water management and climate change issues, they are often siloed and not designed holistically, which negates much of their benefit and can even backfire under some circumstances.

Given that Pakistan is a highly water-stressed nation, water must be treated as an all-year concern, rather than a seasonal issue. Despite improvements in some areas of water management, much work is needed to meet the goals of the National Water Policy of 2018, with the Asian Water Development Outlook 2025 warning that improvement has not kept pace with risk, and implementation remains inconsistent.

But aside from full implementation of the 2018 policy and the 1991 Water Apportionment Accord for the provinces, we need investment in water storage and flood management infrastructure, stronger hydrological cooperation with our neighbours, climate-smart agriculture, and digital overhauls of water accounting and groundwater regulation. Long-term planning should not mean preparing the country for the next flood, but rather, preparing it for the next generation.

title: Innovative policing
author: none@none.com (Mohammad Ali Babakhel)
content:
IN post-colonial societies, police are averse to innovation. Conversely, militants opt for innovation and cultivate their following, using cyberspace, AI and information warfare innovatively. Is innovative policing (IP) viable under outdated laws, weak capacity, poor accountability and ill-equipped LEAs? Post-colonial police chiefs limit innovation to technology when it should be interpreted elastically.
Often, militants get ahead of LEAs; they use drones, night vision goggles, thermal imaging, cyberspace, etc. IP merges tech-driven, community-oriented, problem-oriented and e-policing. Combining traditional police values with modern, evidence-based policing to analyse crime patterns improves public safety and wins community trust, reducing the burden on courts and jails. Policing that doesn’t factor in local needs can be a waste of resources.
    
For IP to succeed, police chiefs and political executives must combine numerical models with technology-led ones rather than rely just on the former. Solutions like drones help LEAs in surveillance; mobile apps improve communication with the public. Deradicalisation and reintegration need collaboration among mental health counsellors, HR advocates and social workers. IP should benefit the public to win its trust and employ new ideas and a community-based approach to law enforcement. A proactive, preventive and participatory mode can help police transition from a force to a service model and boost democratic governance via technology, institutional reforms and enhanced community involvement.
Policing today faces fake news and militants’ misuse of technology. It can improve through transparency, training, independent oversight, investigation and witness cooperation. Police can work with LGs, schools and social services to address violent tendencies, reduce crime, strengthen public trust and enhance fairness in policing.
IP should benefit the public.
Limited finances, few tech-skilled staff and internet disruptions limit innovation. Outdated laws and systems don’t support digital evidence; absent or weak privacy and data protection also hinder innovation. Traditional societies resist change, fearing police may misuse innovation for control and invasion of privacy. A lack of long-term policy vision and reform, together with regular political changes, hinders innovation. Poor outreach limits it too. Corruption undermines transparency. Tech without institutional reform leads to failure.
IP enhances public safety through GPS-enabled patrols and emergency apps, improves monitoring of public places and helps reduce street crime. It boosts trust and police-community ties via engagement, decreases fear and improves service delivery through online FIR and complaint registration. Tech use enables police to improve crime investigation, reducing reliance on coercive means. Helplines and apps for children, women and trans persons improve safety. Technology reduces face-to-face interaction.
Despite security challenges, KP Police have launched innovative public-friendly initiatives. The Nadra-integrated Police Sahulat Markaz Global App offers many services: IGP complaints access, online complaints for FIR, police character certificates, Talash-i-Gumshda, servant verification, Pink Button for women and children, trans persons’ complaint portal (Police Dost), SOS Alert and Police Sahulat counters at hospitals for medico-legal certificates.
    
Japan’s Koban policing includes neighbourhood police stations in communities; police here work with residents and local ins­titutions, boosting public trust and crime prevention. Singapore has developed tech-led ‘sm­art policing’, combining facial recognition, AI-enabled CCTV and smart patrol vehicles, reducing the need for human resources and enhan-cing response times. In the UK, neighbourhood policing teams work with local councils, NGOs and residents to tackle youth issues, an approach that has led to effective local solutions.
Estonia has paperless e-policing and citizen services, including online crime reporting. Scotland’s Violence Reduction Unit addresses violence as a public health issue, fostering collaboration among police and health and education departments. Bodycams during public interaction in some countries have led to increased transparency and reduced misconduct and false allegations. Gender-sensitive policing in Canada and the Nordic states focuses on victims’ unique needs.
Without changes to laws and procedures, transparency in public complaints and training aligned with contemporary challenges, IP cannot become a reality, and technology will fail to win public trust. As described above, the Koban system operates effectively and should be modified for use in Pakistan’s rural areas.
The writer is a security analyst and author of Pakistan: In Between Extremism and Peace.

IP merges tech-driven, community-oriented, problem-oriented, and e-policing to improve public safety, build community trust, enhance service delivery, and reduce the burden on the judicial system.

The success of IP is hampered by outdated laws, weak institutional capacity, poor accountability, limited finances, societal resistance to change, and a lack of long-term policy vision and political will.

For IP to be effective, it requires comprehensive institutional reforms, updated legal frameworks, robust training, enhanced transparency, strong independent oversight, and active community engagement, drawing lessons from international best practices.

title: Water policy
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE country is caught in a crisis where there too much water at the wrong time and too little when it is most needed. The response remains reactive — managing emergencies instead of building resilience against mounting water insecurity. A new report, Water, Climate and Diplomacy: Securing Pakistan’s Indus Basin Future, has rightly called for a national water security policy. The challenge, it says, extends beyond managing rivers and reservoirs. Climate change is altering the hydrological cycle itself. Erratic rainfall, accelerated glacier melt and prolonged droughts are making historical assumptions about water availability unreliable. Pakistan must now stop treating floods, droughts, water scarcity and climate change as separate policy problems. Instead, these should be seen as a single national security challenge.
The report argues that extreme rainfall, inadequate storage, ageing irrigation infrastructure, poor groundwater governance and weak flood preparedness are together increasing Pakistan’s vulnerability and exposing weaknesses in water management. The policy scope should be extended to include the urban dimension, which also needs urgent attention. Cities now routinely face inundation after rainfall because of unplanned expansion, encroachments on natural waterways, inadequate storm-water systems and the loss of open spaces. A national water policy must strengthen urban drainage, protect waterways, enforce land-use rules and promote climate-resilient infrastructure. Agriculture, too, presents a critical challenge, consuming most of the country’s freshwater. Water security ultimately depends on producing more food with less water. This requires a shift from wasteful irrigation towards precision and climate-smart agriculture, improved crop choices, modern irrigation technologies, better water pricing and stronger incentives for conservation. Groundwater is a particularly urgent issue. Unchecked extraction is turning the water crisis into a catastrophe, with aquifers in many areas being depleted faster than they can recharge while pollution further reduces usable supplies. That said, Pakistan’s water and economic security largely hinges on smooth implementation of the Indus Waters Treaty, which has been illegally suspended by India. The country needs sustained global engagement for reversion of this arbitrary action. A national water security policy must therefore integrate water management, agriculture, urban planning, climate resilience and water diplomacy into a single strategy. The cost of reactive policymaking will only rise as climate pressures intensify.

title: Delayed devolution
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE debate over Islamabad’s reluctance to fully let go of devolved subjects has been running since 2010. But it has made little difference to the governments that have come and gone in the meantime. The Senate Standing Committee on Devolution has once again put its finger on the same wound. Fifteen years after the 18th Amendment redrew the administrative and political boundaries between Islamabad and the provinces, the centre continues to run ministries on devolved subjects. The Senate panel is right to call this a constitutional violation dressed up as administrative continuity. The 18th Amendment envisages nine federal ministries. The centre currently has 31. Education, health, food security, culture, climate change, housing and several other subjects that were handed to the provinces still have a federal budget line. The pattern is sustained across governments.
There are two consequences. The first is the erosion of provincial autonomy through a less visible route of parallel bureaucracies. When a federal ministry keeps functioning on a devolved subject, it does not simply duplicate provincial effort; it re-establishes a centre of decision-making that provinces were supposed to have inherited. Policy, funding priorities and technical standard-setting drift back towards Islamabad. The second consequence is fiscal, arguably more damaging in the current climate. The numbers are staggering. The committee noted that federal expenditure has climbed to roughly Rs19tr. It suggested that federal spending be capped at around Rs13tr. This is not an abstract austerity target but a rough estimate of what the federal government would actually need to spend if it confined itself to the ministries the Constitution assigns it. This is where the two problems meet. An oversized federal government does not simply waste money in isolation, it widens the very fiscal deficit that then gets passed back to the provinces to help close. Provinces are routinely asked to deliver cash surpluses, restrain their development spending, and contribute towards ‘critical’ federal debt-servicing targets under IMF-linked fiscal arrangements, even as the federal government keeps funding ministries that have no constitutional business existing. The provinces are, in effect, being asked to subsidise the centre’s refusal to devolve. This is tantamount to federal free-riding financed by the same provinces whose autonomy is undercut.
Published in Dawn, July 27th, 2026

title: Harvest of hope
author: none@none.com (Zofeen T. Ebrahim)
content:
FEW trees carry as much history and symbolism as the olive. In Palestine, it has become a symbol of loss, identity and steadfastness. In Pakistan, by contrast, it reflects hope, promising food and livelihood security in an increasingly hostile climate — not just for today’s farmers, but also future generations of farmers.
What began as a government experiment in olive cultivation two decades ago is finally bearing fruit. This month, a Pakistani startup won a gold medal at the 2026 Dubai International Olive Oil Competition. It had already begun gaining recognition last year when it won a silver medal in the extra virgin olive oil category at the New York International Olive Oil Competition, followed by honours in London and Berlin. With an estimated 10 million acres of land suitable for olive cultivation, Pakistan could eventually rub shoulders with established producers such as Egypt, Tunisia and Morocco, if more people could look towards olive cultivation.
Why olives — and why now? What began in the 1980s, when the Pakistan Agricultural Research Council and provincial research institutes started testing Mediterranean olive varieties, has evolved into more than eight certified nurseries producing domestic olive saplings, 51 processing units, and extra virgin olive oil (EVOO). The journey has been slow, but fairly smooth, even profitable. Italy’s support has been pivotal. Since 2011, it has invested about €5 million, combining funding with technical expertise to establish nurseries, train farmers, improve oil extraction and build laboratories.
In a country where farming is threatened by climate change, water scarcity and rising input costs, the hardy olive offers a rare opportunity. It thrives in rain-fed areas, requires relatively little water once established and produces a high-value crop. Pakistan has become South Asia’s only exporter, with shipments to the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Qatar, as well as smaller consignments to the UK, Canada and Germany. Grown across the Potohar plateau, parts of KP, and smaller plantations in Gilgit-Baltistan and Azad Kashmir, olives are cultivated nationwide. But it is Loralai, in northern Balochistan, that has put Pakistan on the international olive oil map. Its rugged landscape has proved remarkably well suited to the crop. Best of all, the Loralai orchards are not sprayed with pesticide or fertiliser.
Why olives — and why now?
As climate change brings greater water scarcity and erratic rainfall, the drought-tolerant olive is ideally suited to Pakistan’s barani (rain-fed) landscapes, where olive orchards also act as natural carbon sinks, says Shaukat Rasool, CEO of the award-winning startup. While producing one kilogramme of rice requires 3,000-5,000 litres of water and a kilo of sugar 15,000-20,000 litres, Rasool says a litre of olive oil needs just 1,500-2,000 litres under drip irrigation — and virtually none in rain-fed orchards.
The accolades don’t end there. This May, Pakistan became the first South Asian country and the 28th permanent member of the International Olive Council. While IOC membership requires Pakistan to meet international standards for quality, testing, labelling and trade, it also gives it greater credibility in global markets.
Still, this is only the first milestone. Of the seven million olive trees planted across 55,669 acres, just one-fifth are bearing fruit. While Pakistan cannot match Spain, Italy or Tunisia in volume, it can compete in premium EVOO alongside New Zealand, Chile and Uruguay. The domestic market is equally promising. As lifestyle diseases rise and younger consumers become more health-cons­c­ious, doctors inc­re­asingly recommend monounsaturated fats; olive oil fits that healthier pro­file.
However, affordability remains a stumbling block. Despite growing support for locally produced olive oil, it remains beyond the reach of most households. Domestic production must increase before olive oil can become a kitchen staple. Equally important is dispelling the notion that all olive oil varieties are unsuitable for high heat and much-fried desi fare. This can also be encouraged by offering a wider range of products, including table olives.
Pakistan’s olive story may still be in its infancy, but it has already earned international recognition. With the olive policy and action plan in place, the next step should be establishing an olive council to iron out taxation, sustainability and governance issues. Investing in scientific research and extension services to support more than 8,000 farmers and over 100 startups and entrepreneurs, most of them young, should also be among the government’s top priorities.
One tree, two stories: in Palestine, the olive bears witness to loss and resistance; in Pakistan, it has become a symbol of climate resilience, prosperity and food security. 
The writer is an independent journalist based in Karachi.
Published in Dawn, July 27th, 2026

title: Charging for Hormuz
author: none@none.com (Sikander Ahmed ShahSana Afraz)
content:
IRAN is seeking to recalibrate its control over the Strait of Hormuz by regulating maritime traffic and establishing a ‘smart management’ system that includes passage fees for vessels traversing the strait. The principal treaty governing these matters is the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which establishes the legal framework applicable to passage through international straits. It recognises two principal regimes: innocent passage and transit passage.
Under UNCLOS, innocent passage is defined as passage that is “not prejudicial to the peace, good order, or security of the coastal State”. Activities that render passage non-innocent, expressly include any threat or use of force against the sovereignty, territorial integrity, or political independence of the coastal state, or in any other manner in violation of the principles of international law embodied in the Charter of the United Nations. Nevertheless, warships enjoy a customary right to innocent passage through straits used in international navigation in times of peace as recognised in the ICJ Corfu Channel case.
    
Innocent passage is more restrictive of the two regimes and applies within a coastal state’s territorial sea. Ships of all states enjoy the right to innocent passage through territorial seas and such passage must be continuous and expeditious. Under Article 25(3), a coastal state may temporarily suspend innocent passage in specified areas of its territorial sea, without discrimination, where necessary for its security and after due publication.
Article 45 of UNCLOS applies to straits that connect a part of the high seas or an Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) with the territorial sea of another state, thereby extending the innocent -passage regime to such straits used for international navigation. Iran would argue that the Strait of Hormuz falls within this special category of straits, much like the Straits of Tiran. This could, in turn, allow Iran to argue that, in specified areas of its territorial sea rather than throughout the entire strait, and upon giving due notice, it may temporarily suspend the innocent passage of foreign ships, without discrimination in form or fact, where such suspension is essential to protect its security.
Iran’s newly formalised Persian Gulf Strait Authority requires vessels to obtain transit authorisation, submit cargo details and pay fees before entering the Strait of Hormuz.
Under Article 37 of UNCLOS, the transit-passage regime applies to straits used for international navigation between one part of the high seas or an EEZ and another part of the high seas or an EEZ. It grants broader rights than innocent passage: submarines may transit while submerged, aircraft enjoy a right of overflight, and passage may not be suspended by the coastal state.
Iran signed UNCLOS in 1982 but never ratified it. Under Article 34 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, a treaty does not, of itself, create obligations for a state that is not a party to it. As per this view, the legal basis for subjecting Iran to the transit-passage regime established under a treaty it has not ratified is questionable, unless it can be shown that the regime exists as a rule of customary international law — a proposition that, in this case, is not fully established. The US, however, maintains that the right of transit passage is part of customary international law, even though it has not ratified UNCLOS.
    
In 1959, Iran extended its territorial sea to 12 nautical miles, citing security concerns over Hormuz. Upon signing UNCLOS in 1982, it declared that transit passage was not part of customary international law but was, instead, a treaty compromise binding only on state parties.
Iran has maintained this position in its domestic law despite the Revolution. The 1964 Maritime Code, a 1981 decree left un-amended after the conclusion of UNCLOS, the 1993 Act on Marine Areas — which requires prior authorisation for numerous categories of vessels, including warships — and the 2012 amendments, all treat Hormuz as subject only to innocent passage.
Assuming arguendo that the right of transit passage applies, Iran would nevertheless maintain that passage through its territorial sea within the Strait of Hormuz remains governed by the innocent-passage regime, with the right to temporarily suspend for security reasons, particularly against belligerent states such as the US and its allies.
However, the innocent-passage regime prohibits imposing a fee merely for the right of passage. Consequently, any charge imposed solely for passage, or applied discriminatorily, would be legally questionable. Articles 16(4) and 18 of the 1958 Convention on the Territorial Sea and the Contiguous Zone prohibit charges for mere innocent passage through straits. Although Iran and the US are not parties to UNCLOS, it is worth noting that Article 26 of the Convention permits charges only for specific services actually rendered to a foreign vessel during innocent passage and requires that such charges be imposed without discrimination.
Iran’s newly formalised Persian Gulf Strait Authority requires vessels to obtain transit authorisation, submit cargo details and pay fees before entering the Strait of Hormuz. This policy, however, is strongly disputed internationally. Although Iran’s sovereignty supports the exercise of administrative, environmental and customs jurisdiction, international law strictly limits passage fees to reimbursement for specific services actually rendered.
To justify its tolls, Iran points to Turkiye’s fee system under the 1936 Montreux Convention and Egypt’s Suez Canal tolls. Unlike the Bosphorus, however, Hormuz is not governed by an existing multilateral treaty legitimising such fees, and, unlike the Suez Canal, Iran has not demonstrated that it provides dedicated services or maintenance for the strait.
If Iran is able — with or without Oman — to conclude an internationally recognised multilateral treaty, attracting a sufficient number of consenting states, that treaty could provide a legal basis for passage tolls, even if opposed by states such as the US. Without such a widely ratified treaty, Iran may struggle to justify a toll system legally, particularly one that is not linked to services actually provided and that accords preferential treatment to certain states.
Sikander Shah is a professor of law at Lums.
Sana Afraz is an international law expert.
Published in Dawn, July 27th, 2026

whyMatters: This article is crucial for understanding international law, particularly the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), and its application to strategic maritime chokepoints. It highlights contemporary geopolitical disputes over maritime sovereignty, freedom of navigation, and the interpretation of international treaties, directly relevant to regional stability and global trade.
summary: Iran is attempting to assert greater control over the Strait of Hormuz by regulating maritime traffic, requiring transit authorization, and proposing passage fees under a 'smart management' system.

The legal framework for passage through international straits, primarily UNCLOS, establishes two principal regimes: innocent passage (more restrictive, potentially suspendable for security) and transit passage (broader rights, non-suspendable).

Iran, having signed but not ratified UNCLOS, disputes the application of the transit passage regime to Hormuz, arguing it is not customary international law and that the strait should remain under the innocent passage regime within its territorial sea.

International law, including UNCLOS and the 1958 Convention, generally prohibits charges solely for the right of passage, making Iran's proposed tolls legally questionable without specific services rendered or a widely ratified multilateral treaty.

In 1959, Iran extended its territorial sea to 12 nautical miles, citing security concerns over the Strait of Hormuz.

title: Still unprepared
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
EVEN as Pakistan counts around 100 deaths since the onset of the monsoon season on June 26, it is bracing for another spell of heavy rain. The Met Office has forecast widespread rain and thunderstorms through July 28, while the NDMA has warned of rising river levels, flash floods, urban flooding and landslides across large parts of the country.
From Gilgit-Baltistan, where glacial lake outburst floods have severed roads, left tourists stranded and disrupted electricity to Punjab’s inundated cities and swelling rivers, Pakistan is confronting a nationwide emergency rather than a handful of isolated weather events.
    
Lahore has recorded its heaviest rainfall of the season so far, Gujranwala and Sialkot have witnessed extensive flooding, while roads, homes, crops, livestock and public infrastructure have suffered much damage. We are reminded once more of how quickly a weather emergency can become a humanitarian one.
The lesson of the devastating 2022 floods was that climate adaptation must become a permanent function of government. Four years later, many of the same weaknesses persist. Every monsoon exposes clogged drains, encroachments on waterways, fragile buildings, poorly maintained roads, fragmented institutions and delayed relief. Official claims of improved drainage and successful desilting deserve recognition where they have demonstrably reduced waterlogging, but they also warrant scrutiny when major roads remain submerged, sinkholes appear after heavy rain, communities are cut off for days and residents are left to empty flooded homes with buckets.
Climate change is undoubtedly intensifying extreme weather, yet governance failures continue to magnify its human cost. Adaptation cannot consist of emergency meetings and relief announcements alone; it must be reflected in resilient infrastructure, stronger planning and accountable institutions.
    
With more rain forecast, the priority must be to prevent further loss of life. Rescue teams, boats, food, medicines, generators and communications equipment should be pre-positioned in vulnerable districts, while warnings must reach communities in local languages through every available medium. Roads to isolated northern valleys should be restored urgently, with helicopters deployed wherever ground access remains impossible. Power distribution companies must secure hazardous installations, and administrations should close dangerous underpasses, riverbanks and mountain routes before tragedies occur.
Beyond the present emergency, governments should publish district-level flood-risk maps, enforce bans on construction over drains and floodplains, expand glacial monitoring and early-warning systems, and subject preparedness claims to independent audits.
Pakistan cannot prevent the monsoon, but it can stop treating predictable hazards as annual surprises. After all, preparedness is judged not by official briefings, but by lives protected.
Published in Dawn, July 27th, 2026

title: Why coercion doesn’t work
author: none@none.com (Maleeha Lodhi)
content:
WHILE leaders of the hybrid government prioritise foreign engagements and overseas trips, domestic challenges continue to intensify. Public discontent and unrest are mounting across the country but the ruling elite remains detached from this reality.
In much of Balochistan the writ of the state doesn’t exist. Militant violence and terrorism are spiralling out of control. In KP escalation in TTP-sponsored terrorist attacks have left people fearful and distrustful of law enforcement authorities. Last week, lawmakers from both sides of the aisle in the KP Assembly described actions against terrorists as “aimless” and ineffective. Unrest in Azad Jammu and Kashmir is far from over. Elections are approaching but they already lack public credibility. At the national level, the government-opposition stand-off continues to fuel a fraught political environment and deepen polarisation in the country. The PTI-led opposition has called for protests on Aug 5 to mark three years since its leader Imran Khan has been in jail.
    
Meanwhile a nationwide lawyers’ movement is taking shape to protest against the 26th and 27th Constitutional Amendments. The Lawyers Action Committee argues that these amendments have made the judiciary subordinate to the executive and gravely undermined judicial independence. It also demanded probes into alleged “excesses” committed in Balochistan, AJK and Gilgit-Baltistan and release of all political prisoners. Add to this ferment public frustration with the growing cost-of -living burden and power outages during peak summer and the picture is one of growing turmoil with public anger rising against the rulers by the day.
What is the hybrid government’s answer to this? There isn’t one. There certainly isn’t a problem-solving response. Instead, the strategy is denial. Pretend everything is fine. Then attack anyone who says otherwise. To the extent that there is a response, it relies primarily on political repression and coercive measures to manage opposition, unrest and public discontent. But putting a lid on problems doesn’t make them go away.
Authoritarian rule can neither meet Pakistan’s challenges nor make the government secure.
The record is there for everyone to see. Along with undermining judicial independence by controversial constitutional amendments there is a marked descent into authoritarianism. Democracy exists mostly in name. Parliament is little more than a rubber stamp. Freedom of assembly is curbed. The opposition is suppressed with its leaders locked away in jails and given long sentences in dubious cases. The media is controlled with TV channels told what not to broadcast and even who to invite to talk shows. Dissent is silenced. Digital space is restricted. Pressure has been mounted on human rights organisations that impedes their work.
Yet the lesson to be learned from Pakistan’s tortured history is that governments cannot strengthen or secure themselves by such oppressive and strong-arm methods. What counts is legitimacy and public acceptance that actions taken by the government are fair and lawful. But the notion the hybrid ruling elite has of ideal governance is that provided by a ‘hard state’. The aspiration for a hard state has been frequently voiced by the country’s top military and civilian leaders. What does it mean? Leaders who used that expression have never really explained. They seem to want a state that has strong governance, centralised power and the capacity to assure national security. But what they have established is an authoritarian state.
    
The hybrid government has at its disposal an array of coercive instruments that it has used to reinforce its power. But has that helped it achieve the core goals of security, stability and the state’s financial solvency? Not by a long shot. It mistakes a hard state for a competent one. A competent state is an efficiently functioning, trusted state that can secure these goals with public support and of course by a legitimate political leadership. A competent state is one able to effectively perform the core functions of a strong state — collect taxes to run the state, ensure rule of law, maintain order, control the borders and deliver public goods. It is also one in which the instruments of governance are robust and institutions fit for purpose. Trust is an indispensable attribute.
The authoritarian state that has emerged is unable to perform fundamental state functions and is predicated on coercion not trust. Moreover, the aim of its sponsors seems to be the accretion of power rather than the pursuit of public goals. There is another aspect to their flawed assumptions. This relates to the inability to distinguish between power and authority. Power and authority are not the same. Power, however ‘hard’, does not automatically confer authority.
Authority is where power, legitimacy and public purpose intersect. Authority rests on the legitimate exercise of power in the public interest that goes beyond the narrow interests or self-preservation of the ruling elite. The ‘rightful’ use of power, deployed to promote a public agenda, bestows authority. Authority is thus more a relationship with the governed than a capacity. It is based on consent, willingly given, as well as trust, not coercion. Authority also rests critically on credibility.
The question is whether coercion has delivered what the state’s managers want. Has the opposition been eliminated by banning rallies, jailing activists, and blocking its path? Clearly not. It may be in disarray, unable to mobilise and its protests blunted, but its support base and popularity remain intact. Has muzzling the media silenced dissent? Traditional media may be controlled, but social media has become the outlet for free expression and criticism.
Has reliance on kinetic force brought peace to troubled Balochistan? It hasn’t. This is not to say militant violence should go unanswered. But the hard-power approach has failed because it ignores the underlying drivers of the unrest: historical grievances, popular discontent and alienation, poor governance, treatment of Baloch nationalists, and a sense of injustice over both unrepresentative rule and the unfair allocation of resources. No surprise, then, that the province remains in turmoil. In AJK, bans and crackdowns have only hardened protesters and worsened the situation. There are widespread concerns this would undermine Pakistan’s long-standing position on occupied Kashmir.
Authoritarian rule is incapable of resolving Pakistan’s problems or making the government secure. It only lays bare its weakness, its fear, and its rejection of democracy. A strong state is built by empowering citizens, not repressing them.
The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.
Published in Dawn, July 27th, 2026

title: Civil service reform: hollow slogans
author: Dr Syed Akhtar Ali Shah
content:
Civil service reforms have topped the agendas of Pakistan's political parties since inception. For decades, leaders have championed slogans to reorient the bureaucracy, foster specialisation and restructure the state machinery for peak efficiency. despite endless committees, official reports, foreign consultants and modern buzzwords, good governance is still out of reach.

The International Crisis Group has, in one of its reports, stated that "decades of mismanagement, political manipulation and corruption have rendered Pakistan's civil service incapable of providing effective governance and basic public services." In public perceptions, the country's 2.4 million civil servants are widely seen as unresponsive and corrupt, and bureaucratic procedures cumbersome and exploitative. Bureaucratic dysfunction and low capacity undermine governance, paving the way for democratic subversion and extremist destabilisation.

It is, however, also a fact that successive governments committed to initiating reforms driven by encouraging expertise and restructuring the administrative machinery. Not only did they introduce special pay scales such as P-I and P-II to attract professionals, they also invited experts from world-renowned institutions - MIT, Yale, Stanford, Oxford, Cambridge, etc - to advise on reforms in institutions such as the FBR, police and other services. However, no noticeable change could be seen, and inevitably, the system functioned on the same stereotypical model.

The antiquated civil service machinery could not deliver in the past, nor does it have the capacity to deliver in the future, regardless of how many experiments are attempted, unless fundamental changes occur. Mere cosmetic changes will not fix a system whose structure was designed for an agrarian economy.

Administrative cadres - both at the federal and provincial levels - continue to rule the roost. In essence, the generalist Pakistan Administrative Service controls the reins, while specialised cadres remain marginalised.

Although the bureaucracy, under the illusion of reform, coins terms such as e-governance, the Prime Minister's Portal and the Chief Minister's Portal, these gimmicks are only good for optics. While they may provide limited relief to a few, they are superficial. These measures hardly address the deeper structural imbalance. For specialists, the existing bureaucratic system remains a black hole where they find it difficult to prosper, with little prospect of meaningful career progression.

The real catch lies in the Rules of Business and the Appointment and Promotion Rules, along with their attached schedules, around which the whole system revolves and which provide real authority to the administrative secretary. Unless these rules are fundamentally changed, all key administrative positions - and even autonomous bodies - will surely remain under the thumb of administrative cadres. Matters have been further aggravated by routine appointment of serving and retired uniformed personnel to key civilian positions. Such appointments further shrink the space for professionals to move up the ladder within the organisation.

At the federal level, all important institutions - such as the FBR, Planning Commission, Capital Development Authority, National Disaster Management Authority, Port Qasim Authority and WAPDA - are largely headed by officers from the administrative services or the military. The provinces are no different. Senior posts have systematically been included in the schedules of the Appointment and Promotion Rules, thus blocking the vertical promotion of experts. Positions such as Director General of Development Authorities, Director General of Prosecution, Inspector General of Prisons, and Chairmen of Textbook Boards are now out of reach for professionals belonging to relevant specialised cadres.

This contradiction is more glaring in the recruitment and career structures of the police and revenue services. Functional specialisation requires that the system of recruiting supervisory officers for the FBR and police through the CSS should be seriously reconsidered. In the police, recruitment should primarily be done at the Constable and Assistant Sub-Inspector levels, with clear educational criteria and rigorous entry tests. From this professionally recruited base, officers would be able to rise - through merit, training and experience - all the way up to the rank of Inspector General of Police.

Similarly, in the Inland Revenue Service and Customs, recruitment should be done at operational levels, such as inspectors and constables. For these positions, high qualifications and intense competition should be mandated. With proper training, exposure and performance-based promotions, these officers would have a chance to climb to the highest offices, including the Chairman of the FBR. Such a system would create institutional ownership, professional pride, and continuity.

The same pattern and rationale of expertise must also be adopted in other key departments. Departments that inherently require technical and professional knowledge should be headed by professionals from within the relevant disciplines. Engineering-intensive departments such as Irrigation, Public Health Engineering, and Communication and Works must be led by career engineers with proven technical and administrative competence. Similarly, the Health Department should be managed by qualified health professionals, while the Education Department should be led by academic experts with deep experience in teaching, research, and educational management.

Pakistan is brimming with talent and ideas, but the leadership lacks the courage to dismantle entrenched privileges and redesign the system on rational, professional lines. Until recruitment, promotion and leadership structures are aligned to prioritise expertise over generalism, civil service reform will remain a slogan - impressive in speeches, attractive in presentations, but hollow in substance.

Real reform begins not with hollow slogans and the caricature of digital portals, but by revisiting the Rules of Business and providing equal opportunities to all talents to climb to the top.

title: AJK election and beyond
author: none@none.com (Ahmed Bilal Mehboob)
content:
IT seems that the upcoming general election for the legislative assembly of Azad Jammu and Kashmir and its aftermath will be critical both for the AJK, Pakistan and the broader region, unlike any other of the past 11 elections since 1970.
First, the general election 2026 is taking place under the overhang of violent protests organised by the now defunct Joint Awami Action Committee. Although the ongoing agitation is the fourth wave of such protests, it seems to be the most violent and severe. A number of fatalities among both civilians and law-enforcement personnel is just one aspect of the crisis. Although the JAAC has now been declared unlawful under the anti-terrorism law and some of its leaders have been taken into police custody, and despite the fact that at least a part of the leadership adopted a very irresponsible and extremist posture, it is difficult to deny that the JAAC and its 38-point people-centric and anti-elite charter of demands attracted a large segment of the Kashmiri population including the youth (particularly its Gen-Z component).
    
Second, the election is being conducted in the absence of two of the most popular groups. The defunct JAAC is not among the registered political parties of AJK and therefore not contesting. Some of its leaders and members tried to submit their nomination papers for the election as independent candidates but these were reportedly not accepted on one pretext or another. The other popular entity that is not contesting is the PTI which has decided to boycott the election as they see no prospect of a free and fair election. In the AJK elections of 2021, the PTI had secured the largest share (31.4 per cent) of the votes and had formed the government. AJK’s anti-defection law is not as stringent as it is in Pakistan, and, following the PTI’s ouster from the seat of power in Islamabad, many PTI legislators in AJK joined other parties. As a result, the PTI government was ousted from AJK as well. The absence of these two popular forces will likely impact the legitimacy and representative character of the legislative assembly.
Another unique aspect of the election is its planned conduct in three phases — unlike past elections which were held in all the constituencies on the same day. This decision of the AJK election commission is guided by the prevailing law and order conditions. The staggering of elections will allow the deployment of a relatively smaller law-enforcement force. The election in the Poonch (Rawlakot) division is scheduled in the third phase as it has been the most affected by the agitation and happens to be the venue for the current sit-in. The administration may also be hoping that some agreement is reached between the agitators and government by the time the third phase of election is scheduled to take place on Aug 10.
The new legislative assembly will have to deal with some knotty problems right after the election.
Phased polls are not a strange phenomenon though they have not taken place in Pakistan. India’s general elections and most state polls are routinely held in phases. There is, however, a critical difference between the Indian practice and what is planned for the AJK election. The Indian election commission keeps its electronic voting machines (equivalent of our ballot boxes) in safe custody after each phase and the counting begins only after the polling in all phases is complete. The result of elections in one phase, therefore, doesn’t impact the voting preferences in the subsequent phases. This is a critical point, which led to the holding of national and provincial election on the same day in Pakistan since 1997. Earlier, provincial elections were held after about a week after the National Assembly election, by which time the results were known and these impacted voting preferences in the provincial elections.
However, AJK election laws require the preliminary result of the election to be announced ‘immediately’ after the counting is completed in a constituency. The question is, if this system is followed, will the result in the first phase impact the voters’ preferences in the subsequent phases? If the result of all phases is to be declared simultaneously, the safekeeping of ballot boxes will be a major problem and may cast another layer of suspicion over the integrity of election.
The new legislative assembly will have to deal with some knotty problems right after the election. The most critical issue is the future of 12 seats allocated for refugees from occupied Jammu and Kashmir on which election takes place among the refugees settled in various parts of Pakistan. Refugees from these two regions settled in Azad Kashmir are not eligible to vote for these 12 seats. The key demand in the ongoing agitation is the abolition of these seats and restricting the voting rights to only those voters residing in Azad Kashmir. Since any change in the current system requires constitutional amendment, the demand could not be accepted. It stems from an impression that elections to the 12 seats are manipulated by the relevant provincial governments in Pakistan and therefore adversely impact the representative character of the assembly.
More than anything else, the new assembly and mainly the Pakistan government will have to seriously consider the interim representation of AJK in the federal structure of Pakistan. AJK’s people, especially the youth and the Gen-Z segment, are dissatisfied with the current arrangement as AJK has no representation in constitutional forums such as the CCI, NEC, NFC, Irsa etc. whose decisions impact them. To prevent a stronger protest wave, the government of Pakistan may want to seriously debate a de facto provincial status for AJK (and GB) on an interim basis without it adversely affecting Pakistan’s legal stand on the Kashmir dispute.
The writer is president of the Pakistan-based think tank Pildat.

title: Outsourcing security
author: none@none.com (Muhammad Amir Rana)
content:
THE recent outcry by Maulana Fazlur Rehman regarding an unspecified state policy to raise private militias for local protection against terrorists has sparked controversy. Many have accused the maulana of disrespecting those who have sacrificed their lives to protect the homeland.
However, the broader context of his remarks deserves scrutiny: why do states encourage local populations in conflict zones to stand up against violent actors? Take the example of Pakistan. Successive governments have used this tactic —from the then East Pakistan to Balochistan and KP. The core question, and perhaps the crux of the maulana’s argument, is why this policy has failed in most cases.
Known for his sharp political timing, the maulana deliberately chose a platform near Lahore, the political heartland of Punjab, to ensure that his message reached key decision-makers. Yet, his objections to local state-backed civilian militias are far from isolated. Across KP and Balochistan, particularly in the southern districts, from Lakki Marwat to Dera Ismail Khan (the maulana’s core constituency), the locals are attempting to form self-defence militias against terrorist groups like the banned TTP and Hafiz Gul Bahadur’s faction. Tribal elders and political leaders have voiced even stronger criticism of security failures by the state — most recently seen in the Quetta sit-ins organised by the families of slain police personnel.
    
There are certainly instances where local private militias were formed by criminal elements seeking state patronage. Overall, however, the phenomenon of state-backed armed groups, variously termed ‘amn (peace) committees’ and ‘lashkars’, or derogatorily labelled ‘death squads’ and ‘cardholders’, is no longer popular. There are distinct reasons for this shift across both KP and Balochistan.
Why do states encourage local populations in conflict zones to stand up against violent actors?
In KP, the reliance on local militias dates back to the British colonial model of collective responsibility. During the peak of counterterrorism operations between 2007 and 2015, the state reactivated this approach. Tens of thousands of anti-Taliban lashkar members were armed, with the civilian and security leadership fully on board.
It was widely believed that President Asif Ali Zardari strongly favoured the strategy; reports during his first presidential tenure suggested a deal for Chinese small arms to equip KP’s peace committees. Many felt personal tragedy also drove this policy, given the assassination of his wife, Benazir Bhutto, by religiously motivated terrorists. Modelled conceptually after the US-backed ‘Sunni awakening’ against Al Qaeda in Iraq, the policy gained initial traction among communities in the former Fata and Pata regions backed by state funding, arms, and institutional cover.
In the early stages, these militias provided crucial local intelligence and served as a protective shield for the state. However, the model quickly exposed its inherent flaws. Some militias abused their authority and committed atrocities, turning the public sentiment against them. More critically, once security forces cleared key areas, the state began viewing these groups as financial and operational burdens and gradually abandoned them. Furthermore, exposing tactical weaknesses to private militias damaged the state’s image, creating a perception that economically and socially weak terrorists were capable of challenging structured security forces without state consent. This has forced security institutions to review their approach towards private militias.
The abandonment left militia members, ‘cardholders’ and local political figures totally vulnerable. The TTP and Baloch terrorist groups marked peace committee members, militia leaders and allied political workers as priority targets, subjecting them to targeted killing, roadside IEDs and grenade attacks. As per a database managed by the Pak Institute for Peace Studies, the terrorists launched 220 attacks against the members of these militias between 2006 and 2015 and killed 507 and injured another 416, while the figure for Balochistan was 77, in which 66 members of private militias were killed. The PPP was at the centre. Its ally, the Awami National Party, ruled KP. Both parties suffered thousands of casualties as well. At the same time, the terrorists tagged them as enemies for being full partners of the establishment, for crushing them and supporting the foreign occupation forces in Afghanistan. According to the data, the terrorists launched 2,007 attacks against political workers mostly belonging to these two parties and killed 4,068 workers and leaders. Maulana Fazl himself survived multiple suicide attacks, while scores of his party members were killed in Bajaur and the surrounding districts.
Apparently, public trust in this strategy eroded long ago. Elders remember how terrorists had killed hundreds of their members and leaders. After state protection evaporated, many refused to volunteer again. Moreover, unresolved issues following the Fata merger, including mass internal displacement, undelivered development funds and a severely underfunded local police force, have deepened the sense of abandonment in tribal communities.
Simultaneously, political and civil actors in Balochistan have raised concerns over rumours regarding the recruitment of former Afghan security operatives for similar purposes for which private militias have been raised. The use of foreign fighters in internal conflicts is not an alien idea, as the recently Russian-made and backed Wagner Group (now Africa Corps) has earned notoriety in the field, and its foreign fighters have been used in several conflicts in Africa, West Asia and even in Ukraine.
If it is true that Afghan fighters are being replaced with local private militias or merged into existing ones, nothing could be worse; it will only empower criminal elements and foreign agents. These criminal elements, alongside private militias and so-called peace committees, were among the primary drivers of mistrust between the state and society in both KP and Balochistan. Even if this is merely a perception among the populace, the state must address it with a clear answer.
The maulana tapped directly into these deep-seated local grievances. By choosing his moment and venue strategically, he ensured that those shaping Pakistan’s national security policy could not ignore the message.
The writer is a security analyst.
Published in Dawn, July 26th, 2026

title: AI in government
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE Prime Minister’s Office has announced the introduction of an AI-powered digital system and directed ministries to replace paper-based processes with digital workflows. Finally, it has been acknowledged that Pakistan’s bureaucracy cannot continue to rely on endless files, handwritten notes and slow-moving paperwork while governments elsewhere are embracing digital tools. Yet the real significance of the move lies not in the adoption of AI itself, but in whether it helps transform the way government functions. Pakistan has too often treated technology as a solution in its own right. New portals, mobile applications and digital platforms have frequently been launched with much fanfare, only to disappoint because the underlying administrative culture remained unchanged. If departments continue to operate in isolation, if officials remain reluctant to share information, if decisions remain tied up in overlapping approvals and if public records are poorly maintained, AI will merely automate existing weaknesses rather than eliminate them. Successful digital transformation begins with reliable data, clearly defined responsibilities and institutions willing to rethink how they work.
Used wisely, AI could nevertheless improve governance in meaningful ways. It can organise vast quantities of official information, reduce repetitive administrative tasks, identify delays in service delivery and provide policymakers with insights that might otherwise be overlooked. Its greatest value may lie in supporting, rather than replacing, public servants. Citizens could benefit through quicker responses, better access to services and greater transparency. Those gains, however, will depend as much on governance as on technology. Sensitive public data must be protected and automated systems should remain subject to human oversight. AI should support administrative decisions rather than replace human judgement and accountability. Above all, this initiative should be judged by measurable improvements rather than ambitious announcements. If it shortens processing time, reduces opportunities for corruption, strengthens record management and makes services more responsive, it will represent genuine reform. If it simply replaces paper files with electronic ones while preserving the same delays, procedures and habits, the technology will have changed far less than the headlines suggest. Modern government is defined not by the tools it adopts but by the quality of service it delivers.

Successful digital transformation hinges on fundamental prerequisites: reliable data, clearly defined responsibilities, and institutions willing to fundamentally rethink their operational methodologies.

Used judiciously, AI can significantly enhance governance by organizing information, reducing repetitive tasks, identifying service delays, and supporting public servants, provided there is robust governance, data protection, and human oversight.

title: Healing touch needed
author: none@none.com (Tariq Khosa)
content:
SINCE early this month, Balochistan has been reeling from a series of dastardly terror attacks. The nexus of ideologically different banned terrorist groups — the religiously motivated extremists of the TTP and BLA terrorists — poses a grave challenge. The current spate of violence started on July 5, when terrorists managed to reach the fertile Shaban area next to Hanna-Urak in the suburbs of Quetta cantonment, and then launched another attack the next day on the Mangi Dam Ziarat police post at the pumping station. Despite a valiant fight put up by a DSP and 40 policemen, the terrorists, who had attacked in a large numbers, kidnapped and killed 27 ammunition-deficient law-enforcement personnel. Timely reinforcements by the police and FC could have prevented this tragedy.
Meanwhile, an FC convoy was attacked near Khad Kucha, district Mastung, resulting in casualties. In addition, a military contingent in unmarked vehicles was attacked at Bela-Vinder by the BLA’s Majeed Brigade, resulting in casualties in double figures. Clashes in the mineral-rich district of Chagai were also reported, while a suicide attack took place in Khuzdar in which a tribal political leader involved in internecine strife lost 17 of his kinsmen to five attackers who rammed their explosive-laden vehicle into the gate of the fortified compound in Wadh. A three-hour gun battle left 30 injured. In the latest high-profile incident on Thursday, a sessions judge and his guard were killed on the road by assailants. 
Since July 5, there have been more than 40 police, military, FC and civilian casualties, while a total of 121 terrorists have been eliminated. The operation is to continue “until the last terrorist is neutralised” say the state authorities. The government has agreed to constitute a judicial commission to probe the Urak violence and Mangi Dam tragedy. Hopefully, a judge of the high court will probe what led to the violence, in which there were four casualties among the local land owners in the agriculturally rich Shaban area around Killi Babri. The question is, how did the armed terrorist groups get involved? Similarly, Mangi is a project of national interest. It will supply fresh water to Quetta and its cantonment and reduce water shortage by around 20 per cent when operational. FC is deployed at the main dam and other ancillary sites. How come the pumping station post which was recently taken over from the defunct levies, was not being jointly manned by the FC and police, especially in light of the threat alerts issued? The most significant concern is the large number of TTP terrorists who have become active in the vast terrain joining Quetta’s suburbs to the mountainous region linking the northern parts of Balochistan with KP.
During the 1980s, under martial law, Gen Ziaul Haq focused on reconciliation and good governance. The best police and civil administration officers were posted to focus on the administration of justice and service delivery. On promotion as SP and on top of my batch, I was allocated to Balochistan where for the next four years I served as additional SP Quetta, district SP Sibi in charge of the Kachi and Sibi districts and Dera Bugti and Kohlu agencies, and finally as SSP Quetta. We respected the citizens who reciprocated the sentiment. The military, police and civil administration worked for the welfare and progress of the province. Roads were safe for travel. Next, I had the honour of serving as IG Balochistan in 2007 under Gen Musharraf’s military hybrid rule. The entire province was converted into a police jurisdiction replacing the ragtag levies model of rural policing. The issue of missing persons and enforced disappearances became a festering wound in the Baloch psyche. The killing of Nawab Bugti in a cave near Kohlu sparked intense violence.
The experienced Balochistan police chief needs full government support.
After the 2008 elections, the PPP-led federal and provincial governments were unable to stop the kill-and-dump strategy. Mass graves were discovered. Human rights violations multiplied. The conversion to police jurisdiction was reversed. Following the 2013 polls, the PML-N-led government adopted a carrot-and-stick approach to the violence. The first-ever non-sardar chief minister genuinely worked for political reconciliation and met the BLA and BRA leaders in London and Geneva. His efforts were scuttled in 2015. The PTI-led government in 2018 could not change the tough security stance vis-à-vis Balochistan. Since the controversial 2024 elections, the PML-N-led federal and PPP-led provincial governments have actively supported this hard security-stance, with male and female Baloch activists convicted under draconian laws. The roads are unsafe. Trade and business are in decline. Fear rules and violence is widespread. Miscreants are active in the following districts: Turbat, Kalat, Khuzdar, Nushki, Surab, Gwadar, Mastung, Panjgur, Awaran, Kachi/Bolan, Kharan, Chaghi, Kohlu, and Washuk. That’s a huge swathe of land.
Police have been facing a massive challenge since the recent conversion of the entire province to police jurisdiction. The experienced CT-related, KP battle-hardened police chief of Balochistan needs full support from the federal and provincial governments in terms of human resources, infrastructure and equipment. The Zia-era model of good governance is worth consideration: give him the best officers in the ranks of SP and SSP to serve for a fixed tenure of three years. The prime minister must review his decision to depute about 20 serving military officers as district SPs in the insurgency-infested areas. This militarisation of police will be a fiasco.
Balochistan suffers from many missed opportunities and unfulfilled promises. Addressing the crisis effectively requires a two-pronged strategy: decisively eliminating the terrorist threat while proactively addressing the grievances of the local population. As this paper rightly observed, “The long-term solution to Balochistan’s problem remains the political path.” The need for a serious political strategy cannot be ignored anymore. A viable dialogue and political process involving Baloch sub-nationalists and other key political and security stakeholders must be held. The state must also address the province’s socioeconomic problems fairly and urgently, as an entrenched feeling of alienation is driving the youth towards the terrorists. No matter how many we arrest or kill, their numbers are increasing exponentially. The only solution lies in good governance and political dialogue. Let the healing process begin with a reconciliation commission. 
The writer is a former IG of Balochistan Police.
Published in Dawn, July 25th, 2026
